questions.question: What Bible passages teach the doctrine of election?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Eph 1:4-5, Rom 8:29-30, Rom 9:11-13
questions.response:
Here are the passages most frequently cited in discussions of the doctrine of election, grouped by theme.

## Key New Testament Passages

**Romans 8:28–30**: "For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those he predestined, he also called; those he called, he also justified; those he justified, he also glorified." (Often called the "golden chain.")

**Romans 9:6–24**: Paul discusses Jacob and Esau ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated"), God's mercy ("I will have mercy on whom I have mercy"), Pharaoh, and the potter and the clay. This is the most debated chapter on the subject.

**Romans 11:5–7**: "So too, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace."

**Ephesians 1:3–14**: "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world... In love he predestined us for adoption... according to the purpose of his will."

**John 6:37, 44, 65**: "All that the Father gives me will come to me... No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."

**John 10:26–29**: "You do not believe because you are not among my sheep."

**John 15:16**: "You did not choose me, but I chose you."

**John 17:2, 6, 9**: Jesus prays for those the Father "has given" him.

**Acts 13:48**: "And as many as were appointed to eternal life believed."

**2 Thessalonians 2:13**: "God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved."

**2 Timothy 1:9**: Grace "given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began."

**1 Peter 1:1–2**: "Elect... according to the foreknowledge of God the Father."

**1 Peter 2:9**: "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood."

**Also relevant:** Matthew 22:14 ("many are called, but few are chosen"), Matthew 24:22, 24, 31, Mark 13:20, 1 Thessalonians 1:4, Titus 1:1, James 2:5, 2 Peter 1:10, and Revelation 13:8 and 17:8 (names written in the book of life "before the foundation of the world").

## Old Testament Background

- **Deuteronomy 7:6–8** and **10:15**: God chose Israel not because of its size or merit but because of his love.
- **Genesis 12:1–3**: The call of Abraham.
- **Isaiah 41:8–9; 43:10; 45:4**: Israel as God's chosen servant.
- **Malachi 1:2–3**: "I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated" (quoted in Romans 9).
- **Exodus 33:19**: "I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious."

## Passages Often Raised in Balance

These are frequently cited regarding God's universal saving desire and human responsibility:
- **1 Timothy 2:3–4**: God "desires all people to be saved."
- **2 Peter 3:9**: "Not wishing that any should perish."
- **John 3:16** and **Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11**.
- **Matthew 23:37**: "How often I wanted to gather your children... and you were not willing."

## A Note on Interpretation

Christians broadly agree that Scripture teaches election but differ on its nature:

- **Reformed/Calvinist** readings see these texts as teaching unconditional, individual election to salvation based solely on God's sovereign will.
- **Arminian/Wesleyan** readings typically understand election as conditional, based on God's foreknowledge of faith.
- **Corporate election** views (common in some Arminian and New Perspective scholarship) see election primarily as God choosing a people "in Christ," with individuals joining that people through faith.
- **Lutheran** theology affirms election to salvation but rejects double predestination, holding the tension unresolved.
- **Catholic and Orthodox** traditions affirm predestination while emphasizing human cooperation with grace.

If you'd like, I can go deeper into a specific passage, such as Romans 9 or Ephesians 1, and how different traditions interpret it.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 10:28-29, Rom 8:38-39, Phil 1:6
questions.response:
The doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, most associated with Reformed theology, holds that those truly regenerated by God will be kept in faith to the end and finally saved. Proponents draw on several groups of texts.

## 1. Christ's promise to keep His sheep
- **John 10:27–29**: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand… no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
- **John 6:37–40**: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out… that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
- **John 17:11–12, 24**: Jesus prays that the Father would keep those given to Him and that they would be with Him where He is.

## 2. God finishes what He begins
- **Philippians 1:6**: "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ."
- **Romans 8:29–30**: The "golden chain." Those foreknown, predestined, called, and justified are also glorified, with no one dropping out between links.
- **1 Corinthians 1:8–9**: God "will sustain you to the end, guiltless… God is faithful."
- **1 Thessalonians 5:23–24**: "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it."

## 3. Nothing can separate believers from God's love
- **Romans 8:31–39**: "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?… Neither death nor life… nor anything else in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus."

## 4. Believers are guarded by God's power
- **1 Peter 1:3–5**: An inheritance "kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed."
- **Jude 24**: "To him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless…"
- **2 Timothy 1:12; 4:18**: "He is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me."

## 5. The sealing and pledge of the Spirit
- **Ephesians 1:13–14**: Believers are "sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it."
- **Ephesians 4:30** (sealed "for the day of redemption") and **2 Corinthians 1:21–22**.

## 6. Christ's ongoing priestly work
- **Hebrews 7:25**: "He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them."
- **Hebrews 10:14**: "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified."
- **Luke 22:31–32**: Jesus prays for Peter "that your faith may not fail."

## 7. The New Covenant promise
- **Jeremiah 32:40**: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me."
- **Ezekiel 36:26–27**: God gives a new heart and His Spirit, and "cause[s] you to walk in my statutes."

## 8. Apostasy as evidence of never truly belonging
- **1 John 2:19**: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us."

## The human side: perseverance, not mere preservation
Reformed theologians stress that the doctrine is about *persevering* in faith and holiness, not "once saved, always saved" regardless of how one lives. Texts like **Colossians 1:22–23** ("if indeed you continue in the faith"), **Hebrews 3:14**, **Matthew 24:13**, and **Philippians 2:12–13** are read as the means God uses to keep His people. Warnings and exhortations are how He preserves them, and continuing in faith is the evidence of genuine conversion.

## Texts raised by other traditions
Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox, and many Lutheran Christians believe true believers *can* fall away. They point to **Hebrews 6:4–6**, **Hebrews 10

questions.question: What verses support the doctrine of total depravity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:10-12, Eph 2:1-3, Gen 6:5
questions.response:
# Key Verses Cited for Total Depravity

Total depravity is the first point of the Reformed "TULIP." It doesn't mean people are as evil as they could be. It means sin has corrupted every part of human nature (mind, will, emotions) so that, apart from God's grace, people cannot and will not turn to God on their own. These are the passages Reformed theologians most often cite.

## Universal Sinfulness
- **Romans 3:10–12**: "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside..." (quoting Psalms 14 and 53)
- **Romans 3:23**: "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
- **Ecclesiastes 7:20**: "Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins."
- **1 Kings 8:46**: "...for there is no one who does not sin."

## Sin from Birth
- **Psalm 51:5**: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me."
- **Psalm 58:3**: "The wicked are estranged from the womb..."
- **Genesis 8:21**: "...the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth."

## Corruption of the Heart and Mind
- **Genesis 6:5**: "...every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually."
- **Jeremiah 17:9**: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
- **Mark 7:21–23**: Evil comes "from within, out of the heart of man."
- **Ephesians 4:17–18**: Gentiles walk "in the futility of their minds... darkened in their understanding... due to their hardness of heart."
- **Titus 1:15**: "...both their minds and their consciences are defiled."

## Spiritual Death
- **Ephesians 2:1–3**: "You were dead in the trespasses and sins... by nature children of wrath."
- **Colossians 2:13**: "And you, who were dead in your trespasses..."
- **Romans 5:12**: Sin and death spread to all through one man (Adam).

## Inability and Bondage of the Will
- **John 6:44**: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."
- **John 6:65**: "No one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
- **Romans 8:7–8**: "The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God... it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God."
- **1 Corinthians 2:14**: "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God... and he is not able to understand them."
- **John 8:34**: "Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
- **Jeremiah 13:23**: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil."
- **John 3:19–20**: People "loved the darkness rather than the light."

## Even "Good" Works Are Tainted
- **Isaiah 64:6**: "All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment."
- **Romans 14:23**: "Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin."

## A Note on Other Views
Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic, and Eastern Orthodox Christians read many of these passages differently. Arminians and Wesleyans generally affirm human corruption but argue that "prevenient grace" restores the ability to respond to God. Orthodox theology rejects the idea of inherited guilt. Catholics teach that human nature is wounded but not totally corrupted. They point to passages such as Deuteronomy 30:19, Joshua 24:15, and Revelation 22:17, which call people to choose.

If you're interested, I can go deeper on any of these passages or on how the debate over them plays out.

questions.question: Which passages teach justification by faith alone?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:28, Eph 2:8-9, Gal 2:16
questions.response:
Justification by faith alone (*sola fide*) is mainly associated with Protestant theology, especially Luther and Calvin. These are the passages most often cited in its support:

## Core Pauline Texts

**Romans 3:21–28** is probably the central passage.
- v. 24: "being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus"
- v. 28: "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law." (Luther famously added "alone," *allein*, in his German translation, arguing it captured the sense.)

**Romans 4:1–8** uses Abraham as the model.
- v. 3: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness" (quoting Genesis 15:6)
- v. 5: "And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness."

**Romans 5:1**: "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

**Galatians 2:16**: "...a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ... because by works of the law no one will be justified."

**Galatians 3:6–14** returns to Abraham and Genesis 15:6 and cites Habakkuk 2:4, "The righteous shall live by faith."

**Ephesians 2:8–9**: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast."

**Philippians 3:8–9**: "...not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith."

## Supporting Texts

- **Titus 3:5–7**: "he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy... being justified by his grace"
- **Romans 10:9–10**: believing in the heart results in righteousness
- **Romans 11:6**: "if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"
- **Luke 18:9–14**: the tax collector "went down to his house justified"
- **John 3:16, 5:24, 6:47**: eternal life through believing
- **Acts 13:38–39** and **Acts 16:31**

## The Main Counter-Text

**James 2:14–26**, especially v. 24: "You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone." This is the only place in Scripture where the phrase "faith alone" appears, and it is negated.

Interpretations differ:
- **Protestants** typically argue that James addresses *demonstrating* genuine faith before others, while Paul addresses standing before God. On this view, true faith inevitably produces works.
- **Catholics and Orthodox** generally hold that justification involves faith working through love (Galatians 5:6) and that works done in grace contribute to final justification. The Council of Trent explicitly rejected *sola fide*.

## Other Scholarly Debate

The **New Perspective on Paul** (E.P. Sanders, N.T. Wright, James Dunn) argues that "works of the law" refers mainly to Jewish identity markers such as circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath, rather than moral effort in general. This reframes what Paul was arguing against.

Would you like me to expand on any of these passages or interpretive traditions?

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 5:12, Rom 5:18-19, Ps 51:5, Gen 3:6-7
questions.response:
The doctrine of original sin holds that Adam's first sin affected all his descendants, leaving humanity in a fallen condition. Different traditions describe that condition differently: as inherited guilt, inherited corruption, or inherited mortality. These are the passages most often cited:

## Primary Texts

**Romans 5:12–21**: The central passage.
- v. 12: "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned..."
- v. 18–19: "One trespass led to condemnation for all men... by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners."
- Paul parallels Adam and Christ: as Adam's act affected all humanity, so Christ's righteousness brings justification.

**1 Corinthians 15:21–22**: "For as by a man came death... For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive."

**Genesis 3**: The account of the Fall itself, including the curse and expulsion from Eden, which brings consequences that extend to Adam and Eve's descendants.

## Texts on Universal or Inborn Sinfulness

- **Psalm 51:5**: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me."
- **Psalm 58:3**: "The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth."
- **Genesis 6:5 and 8:21**: "The intention of man's heart is evil from his youth."
- **Ephesians 2:1–3**: "...and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind."
- **Job 14:4**: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one."
- **Job 15:14** and **Job 25:4**: Questions about how one "born of a woman" can be pure.
- **Jeremiah 17:9**: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick."
- **Romans 3:9–23**: "None is righteous, no, not one... for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
- **Romans 7:14–25**: Paul's description of indwelling sin.
- **John 3:5–6**: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh," which implies the need for new birth.
- **Ecclesiastes 7:20 and 7:29**: "God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes."

## Interpretive Notes

- **Romans 5:12's "because all sinned"** (Greek *eph' hō*) is heavily debated. Augustine, relying on the Latin "in whom," read it as all sinning *in Adam*. Many modern scholars translate it "because" and see it as referring to personal sin as well.
- **Catholic and Reformed** traditions generally affirm inherited guilt and corruption. Reformed theology often frames this through federal headship (Adam as humanity's representative).
- **Eastern Orthodox** theology usually speaks of "ancestral sin": inheriting mortality and a disordered nature rather than Adam's personal guilt.
- **Critics**, from Pelagius to some modern theologians, argue these texts describe universal sinfulness or Adam's bad influence rather than an inherited condition. They also point to passages like **Ezekiel 18:20** ("The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father").
- **Jewish interpretation** generally does not read Genesis 3 as teaching original sin. It speaks instead of the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination).

If you'd like, I can go deeper into any one passage or tradition's reading.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The word "Trinity" doesn't appear in the Bible, and no single verse lays out the full doctrine. Trinitarian Christians see it as a synthesis of several biblical teachings that, taken together, lead to the conclusion that one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The doctrine was formally articulated at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).

## 1. There is only one God
- **Deuteronomy 6:4** – "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one."
- **Isaiah 45:5** – "I am the LORD, and there is no other; besides me there is no God."
- **1 Corinthians 8:4–6**, **James 2:19**

## 2. The Father is God
- **John 6:27**, **1 Corinthians 8:6**, **Galatians 1:1** (This point is rarely disputed.)

## 3. The Son is God
- **John 1:1, 14** – "The Word was God… and the Word became flesh."
- **John 20:28** – Thomas calls Jesus "My Lord and my God."
- **Philippians 2:5–11** – Christ existed "in the form of God" and receives the worship due to Yahweh (echoing Isaiah 45:23).
- **Colossians 2:9** – "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."
- **Hebrews 1:8** – The Father addresses the Son as "God."
- **Titus 2:13**, **2 Peter 1:1** – "our God and Savior Jesus Christ."
- **John 8:58** – "Before Abraham was, I am."

## 4. The Holy Spirit is God and personal
- **Acts 5:3–4** – Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.
- **1 Corinthians 2:10–11** – The Spirit knows the thoughts of God.
- **John 14–16** – The Spirit teaches, testifies, and guides, and is referred to as a personal Helper.
- **Ephesians 4:30** – The Spirit can be grieved.

## 5. Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct
- **Matthew 3:16–17** – At Jesus's baptism, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks.
- **John 14:16–17** – Jesus asks the Father to send "another Helper."
- **John 17** – The Son prays to the Father.

## 6. The three are named together as equals
- **Matthew 28:19** – Baptize "in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
- **2 Corinthians 13:14** – "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit…"
- **1 Peter 1:2**, **Ephesians 4:4–6**

## Old Testament passages often cited as hints
- **Genesis 1:26** – "Let *us* make man in *our* image."
- **Isaiah 48:16**, **Isaiah 63:9–10**, and the figure of the "Angel of the LORD."

Many scholars, including some Trinitarians, see these as suggestive rather than conclusive.

## A note on 1 John 5:7
The King James Version reads "the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one." This phrase (the *Comma Johanneum*) is absent from early Greek manuscripts and is widely recognized as a later addition, so most modern translations omit it.

## Other views
Not all who read the Bible accept the Trinity:
- **Unitarians** and **Biblical Unitarians** affirm one God, the Father, and see Jesus as a human Messiah.
- **Jehovah's Witnesses** view Jesus as a created being, God's first creation.
- **Oneness Pentecostals** see Father, Son, and Spirit as modes or manifestations of one person.

These groups offer alternative readings of the passages above, for example by translating John 1:1 differently or interpreting texts like John 14:28 ("the Father is greater than I") and Mark 13:32 as evidence against Jesus's full equality with the Father.

If you'd like, I can go deeper into any particular passage, the historical development at the early councils, or the arguments between Trinitarian and non-Trinitarian interpreters.

questions.question: What passages affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 1:1, John 1:14, Col 2:9, Heb 1:3, Phil 2:6
questions.response:
Christian theologians commonly cite these passages in support of the full deity of Jesus Christ, grouped by the kind of claim they make.

## Direct Statements Calling Jesus "God"

- **John 1:1, 14**: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh."
- **John 20:28**: Thomas addresses the risen Jesus: "My Lord and my God!" Jesus accepts the confession.
- **Romans 9:5**: "…the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever."
- **Titus 2:13**: "…our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."
- **2 Peter 1:1**: "…the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ."
- **Hebrews 1:8**: The Father says of the Son, "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" (quoting Psalm 45:6).
- **1 John 5:20**: "…his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life."
- **John 1:18**: In many early manuscripts, "the only God, who is at the Father's side."

## Jesus Sharing God's Nature and Glory

- **Colossians 2:9**: "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."
- **Colossians 1:15–17**: He is the image of the invisible God, and all things were created through him and for him.
- **Hebrews 1:3**: "He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature."
- **Philippians 2:5–11**: Christ existed "in the form of God" and had "equality with God."
- **John 17:5**: Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father "before the world existed."

## Divine Names and Self-Identification

- **John 8:58**: "Before Abraham was, I am." His hearers attempt to stone him, echoing Exodus 3:14.
- **John 10:30–33**: "I and the Father are one." His opponents respond that he, a man, makes himself God.
- **John 5:18**: He was "making himself equal with God."
- **Revelation 1:8, 17; 22:13**: "The Alpha and the Omega… the first and the last," a title Isaiah 44:6 applies to YHWH.

## Old Testament YHWH Texts Applied to Jesus

- **Isaiah 6:1–10 → John 12:41**: Isaiah "saw his glory."
- **Isaiah 45:23 → Philippians 2:10–11**: Every knee will bow to Jesus.
- **Joel 2:32 → Romans 10:9–13**: "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
- **Psalm 102:25–27 → Hebrews 1:10–12**: The Son as eternal Creator.
- **Isaiah 40:3 → Mark 1:2–3**: Preparing the way of the LORD is applied to preparing for Jesus.

## Divine Works and Prerogatives

- **Creation**: John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2
- **Forgiving sins**: Mark 2:5–7 ("Who can forgive sins but God alone?")
- **Sustaining the universe**: Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:17
- **Final judgment**: John 5:22–23; 2 Corinthians 5:10
- **Giving eternal life**: John 10:28; 11:25

## Receiving Worship

- **Matthew 14:33; 28:9, 17**: The disciples worship Jesus.
- **Hebrews 1:6**: "Let all God's angels worship him."
- **Revelation 5:11–14**: The Lamb receives the same worship as the One on the throne.
- Contrast **Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9** and **Acts 10:25–26**, where angels and apostles refuse worship.

## Divine Attributes

- **Eternality**: Micah 5:2; John 1:1–2
- **Omniscience**: John 2:24–25; 16:30; 21:17
- **Omnipresence**: Matthew 18:20; 28:20
- **Immutability**: Hebrews 13:8

## A Note on Interpretation

Some of these texts involve debated translation or textual questions, such as Romans 9:5 (punctuation), John 1:18 (manuscript variants), and the Granville Sharp construction in Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1. Groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses and Unitarians read several of them differently. Orthodox Christian theology has generally argued that the cumulative weight of these passages, rather than any single verse, establishes Christ's full deity. That conclusion was formalized at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451).

Recommended resources include Murray Harris's *Jesus as God*, Richard Bauckham's *Jesus and the God of Israel*, and Bowman and Komoszewski's *Putting Jesus in His Place*.

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 15:3-8, Matt 28:5-6, Luke 24:39, John 20:27
questions.response:
Here are the main biblical passages that teach or support the bodily (physical) resurrection of Jesus, grouped by theme.

## 1. The Empty Tomb
The body that was buried is the body that was raised. Nothing was left behind.
- **Matthew 28:1–10**: The angel says, "He is not here; for he has risen… Come, see the place where he lay."
- **Mark 16:1–8**: "He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him."
- **Luke 24:1–12**: The women find the stone rolled away and the body gone. Peter sees "the linen cloths by themselves."
- **John 20:1–10**: Peter and John see the grave cloths lying there, with the face cloth folded separately.
- **Matthew 28:11–15**: The guards are bribed to say the disciples stole the body. This tacitly concedes the tomb was empty.

## 2. Jesus' Physical Appearances
These are the clearest texts for a *bodily* rather than merely spiritual resurrection.
- **Luke 24:36–43**: "Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have." He then eats broiled fish in front of them.
- **John 20:19–20**: He shows the disciples his hands and his side.
- **John 20:24–29**: Thomas is invited to put his finger in the nail marks and his hand in Jesus' side.
- **John 21:9–14**: Jesus cooks breakfast and eats with the disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
- **Matthew 28:9**: The women "took hold of his feet and worshiped him."
- **Luke 24:13–35**: He walks with the Emmaus disciples and breaks bread with them.
- **Acts 1:3**: "He presented himself alive… by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days."
- **Acts 10:40–41**: The apostles "ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."

## 3. Jesus' Own Predictions
- **John 2:19–22**: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… He was speaking about the temple of his body."
- **Matthew 12:39–40**: The sign of Jonah.
- **Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34**: The repeated predictions that he would be killed and rise after three days.
- **John 10:17–18**: "I lay down my life that I may take it up again."

## 4. Apostolic Preaching in Acts
- **Acts 2:24–32**: Peter cites Psalm 16. David's body decayed, but Christ's "flesh did not see corruption."
- **Acts 13:29–37**: Paul makes the same argument. David "saw corruption," but "he whom God raised up did not."
- **Acts 17:31**: God has given assurance to all "by raising him from the dead."

## 5. The Epistles
- **1 Corinthians 15:3–8**: The early creed: "he was buried… he was raised on the third day," followed by a list of eyewitnesses, including more than 500 at once.
- **1 Corinthians 15:12–20**: "If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile."
- **1 Corinthians 15:35–49**: The resurrection body is a transformed "spiritual body" (*sōma pneumatikon*). Most scholars understand this as a body animated by the Spirit, not an immaterial one.
- **Romans 1:4; 6:9; 8:11**: Christ was raised and "will never die again," and the same Spirit "will also give life to your mortal bodies."
- **Philippians 3:20–21**: Christ "will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body."
- **Colossians 2:9**: "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."
- **1 John 1:1**: "…which we have seen with our eyes… and touched with our hands."

## 6. Old Testament Anticipations
- **Psalm 16:10**: "You will not… let your holy one see corruption." The apostles apply this verse to Jesus.
- **Isaiah 53:10–12**: After the Servant's death, "he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days."
- **Jonah 1:17**: Cited by Jesus as a sign (Matthew 12:40).

## 7. The Risen and Exalted Christ
- **Revelation 1:17–18**: "I died, and behold I am alive forevermore."
- **Acts 1:9–11**: He ascends bodily and "will come in the same way."

**Key point:** The strongest texts for the *bodily* nature of the resurrection are **Luke 24:39–43**, **John 20:27**, **Acts 2:31**, and **1 Corinthians 15:3–4**. They combine the empty tomb, the continuity of the crucifixion wounds, and physical actions such as touching and eating.

questions.question: What Scripture supports the doctrine of substitutionary atonement?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Isa 53:5-6, 2 Cor 5:21, 1 Pet 2:24, Rom 3:25
questions.response:
Substitutionary atonement is the teaching that Christ died in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty or consequence of their sin. Supporters typically draw on the following passages.

## Old Testament Foundations

**The sacrificial system**
- **Leviticus 16** – On the Day of Atonement, the high priest lays hands on the scapegoat and confesses Israel's sins over it, and it "shall bear all their iniquities on itself" (16:21–22).
- **Leviticus 17:11** – "The life of the flesh is in the blood… it is the blood that makes atonement by the life."
- **Leviticus 1:4** – Laying a hand on the burnt offering so it is "accepted for him to make atonement for him."

**Typological episodes**
- **Genesis 22** – God provides a ram in place of Isaac.
- **Exodus 12** – The Passover lamb's blood spares the firstborn (cf. 1 Cor. 5:7).

**The Suffering Servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12)**, often considered the central OT text:
- "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace" (53:5).
- "The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (53:6).
- "He shall bear their iniquities" (53:11); "he bore the sin of many" (53:12).

## Gospels

- **Mark 10:45 / Matthew 20:28** – "The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom *for* (Greek *anti*, 'in place of') many."
- **Matthew 26:28** – "My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."
- **John 1:29** – "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
- **John 10:11, 15** – The good shepherd "lays down his life for the sheep."
- **John 11:50–52** – Caiaphas unwittingly prophesies that one man should die for the people.
- **Mark 15:34** – The cry of dereliction, often read as Christ bearing divine judgment.

## Pauline Epistles

- **Romans 3:23–26** – God put Christ forward as a "propitiation" (*hilastērion*) by his blood, so that he might be "just and the justifier."
- **Romans 4:25** – "Delivered up for our trespasses."
- **Romans 5:6–10** – "Christ died for the ungodly… while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
- **Romans 8:3** – God "condemned sin in the flesh" by sending his Son "for sin."
- **1 Corinthians 15:3** – "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures."
- **2 Corinthians 5:21** – "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." This is a key "great exchange" text.
- **Galatians 3:13** – "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us."
- **Ephesians 5:2** – Christ "gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God."
- **Colossians 2:13–14** – The record of debt was nailed to the cross.
- **1 Timothy 2:6** – He "gave himself as a ransom (*antilytron*) for all."
- **Titus 2:14** – He "gave himself for us to redeem us."

## Hebrews

- **Hebrews 9:12–14, 22, 26–28** – "Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness"; Christ was "offered once to bear the sins of many."
- **Hebrews 10:10–14** – Sanctified "through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all."
- **Hebrews 2:17** – He became a merciful high priest "to make propitiation for the sins of the people."

## General Epistles

- **1 Peter 2:24** – "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree" (echoing Isaiah 53).
- **1 Peter 3:18** – "Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God."
- **1 John 2:2** – "He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world."
- **1 John 4:10** – God "sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins."

## Revelation

- **Revelation 1:5; 5:9** – "Freed us from our sins by his blood"; "by your blood you ransomed people for God."

## A Note on Interpretation

Christians broadly agree that these texts teach Christ died "for us" and "for our sins." They differ on the precise mechanism:

- **Penal substitution** (emphasized in Reformed and evangelical theology) holds that Christ bore the legal penalty of God's wrath in our place. It leans heavily on Isaiah 53, Romans 3, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Galatians 3:13.
- **Other substitutionary or representative views** (e.g., Anselm's satisfaction theory, and some Catholic and Orthodox readings) affirm that Christ acted on our behalf but frame it in terms of honor, healing, participation, or covenant representation.
- **Debated points** include whether *hilastērion* means "propitiation" (appeasing wrath) or "expiation" (removing sin), and whether *hyper* ("for") implies strict replacement or broader benefit.
- Many theologians hold substitution alongside other biblical themes, such as **Christus Victor** (Col. 2:15; Heb. 2:14) and moral example (1 Pet. 2:21), rather than in opposition to them.

If you'd like, I can go deeper into any one passage, the Greek terms involved, or how different traditions handle these texts.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 2 Cor 5:21, Rom 4:3-6, Phil 3:9, Rom 5:19
questions.response:
# Biblical Basis for the Imputation of Christ's Righteousness

The doctrine (central to Reformed and Lutheran theology) holds that believers are declared righteous before God because Christ's righteousness is *credited* to them, not because of any righteousness inherent in themselves. No single verse states the full doctrine in those words. It is built from several texts read together.

## Key New Testament Texts

**Romans 4:3–8**
Paul cites Genesis 15:6, "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness," and uses the accounting term *logizomai* (to credit or reckon) repeatedly. He links it with Psalm 32: "Blessed is the man… to whom God counts righteousness apart from works… against whom the Lord will not count his sin." This is the clearest passage for righteousness being *reckoned* rather than earned.

**Romans 5:12–21**
The Adam–Christ parallel is often considered the strongest structural argument. Just as Adam's one act of disobedience brought condemnation to those "in him," Christ's obedience brings justification to those "in him." Verse 19 says, "By the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous." Verse 17 speaks of "the free gift of righteousness." Defenders argue that the representative logic only works if Christ's obedience is credited to others, much as Adam's sin was.

**2 Corinthians 5:21**
"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." This is the basis for "double imputation": our sin is reckoned to Christ, and his righteousness to us.

**Philippians 3:8–9**
Paul wants to be "found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith." Here righteousness is described as coming from outside the believer (an *alien* righteousness).

**1 Corinthians 1:30**
"Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption."

**Romans 3:21–26 and 10:3–4**
These passages describe a righteousness of God "apart from the law" given through faith, and contrast it with seeking to establish "their own" righteousness.

## Old Testament Background Often Cited

- **Genesis 15:6**: Abraham's faith counted as righteousness.
- **Isaiah 61:10**: "He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness."
- **Zechariah 3:1–5**: The high priest Joshua's filthy garments are removed and replaced with clean ones, a picture of guilt removed and righteousness given.
- **Jeremiah 23:6**: The coming king is called "The LORD is our righteousness."
- **Isaiah 53:11**: "By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities."

## How the Argument Fits Together

1. God requires perfect righteousness (e.g., Gal 3:10; Matt 5:48).
2. Humans lack it (Rom 3:10, 23).
3. Justification is a legal declaration, not a moral transformation. The contrast with "condemnation" in Romans 5:16, 18 and 8:33–34 supports this.
4. That declaration is based on a righteousness credited from outside us, specifically Christ's, through union with him ("in him").

## Points of Debate

- **Roman Catholic and Orthodox theology** generally emphasize righteousness that is *infused* or participatory rather than merely imputed, though both affirm justification by grace.
- **N.T. Wright and some New Perspective scholars** argue that "the righteousness of God" means God's own covenant faithfulness, which isn't the kind of thing transferred to others. On this view, justification is God's declaration of covenant membership, and union with Christ, not imputation, is the key category.
- **Some Protestants** (e.g., Robert Gundry) argue that Romans 4 says *faith* is counted as righteousness, not Christ's righteousness specifically. Others accept imputation of forgiveness but question the imputation of Christ's "active obedience" (his lifelong law-keeping).

## Further

questions.question: What passages describe the process of sanctification?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Thess 4:3, Phil 2:12-13, 2 Cor 3:18, Heb 12:14
questions.response:
Sanctification, the process of being made holy, is described throughout the New Testament, with roots in the Old. Here are key passages grouped by theme.

## Sanctification as God's Work
- **1 Thessalonians 5:23–24**: "May God himself, the God of peace, sanctify you through and through... The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it."
- **Philippians 1:6**: "He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus."
- **Philippians 2:12–13**: "Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you to will and to act." This passage pairs human effort with divine enabling.
- **Hebrews 13:20–21**: God equips believers and works in them "what is pleasing to him."

## Transformation and Growth
- **Romans 12:1–2**: "Be transformed by the renewing of your mind."
- **2 Corinthians 3:18**: Believers "are being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit."
- **2 Peter 1:3–8**: A progression of virtues (faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, mutual affection, love) that believers are to "make every effort" to add.
- **2 Peter 3:18**: "Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ."
- **Ephesians 4:11–16**: The church grows to maturity, "attaining to the whole measure of the fullness of Christ."

## Putting Off the Old, Putting On the New
- **Ephesians 4:22–24**: Put off the old self, be renewed in mind, put on the new self "created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness."
- **Colossians 3:1–17**: Set minds on things above, "put to death" earthly practices, and clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, and love.
- **Romans 6**: Dying to sin and living to God; offering oneself as an instrument of righteousness "leading to holiness" (v. 19, 22).

## The Spirit's Role
- **Galatians 5:16–25**: Walking by the Spirit versus the flesh; the fruit of the Spirit.
- **Romans 8:1–17**: Life in the Spirit; "by the Spirit you put to death the misdeeds of the body" (v. 13).
- **2 Thessalonians 2:13**: Salvation "through the sanctifying work of the Spirit."
- **1 Peter 1:2**: Chosen "through the sanctifying work of the Spirit."

## Holiness as Calling and Command
- **1 Thessalonians 4:3–7**: "It is God's will that you should be sanctified."
- **1 Peter 1:14–16**: "Be holy, because I am holy" (quoting Leviticus 11:44; 19:2).
- **Hebrews 12:10–14**: God disciplines "that we may share in his holiness"; "pursue... holiness, without which no one will see the Lord."
- **2 Corinthians 7:1**: "Perfecting holiness out of reverence for God."

## Means of Sanctification
- **John 17:17**: "Sanctify them by the truth; your word is truth."
- **Romans 5:3–5 and James 1:2–4**: Suffering produces perseverance, character, and maturity.
- **Hebrews 10:24–25**: Mutual encouragement in community.

## Positional vs. Progressive Sanctification
Some passages present sanctification as already accomplished:
- **1 Corinthians 6:11**: "You were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified."
- **Hebrews 10:10, 14**: "We have been made holy... he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy." Verse 14 holds both aspects together.
- **1 Corinthians 1:2**: "Those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be his holy people."

## Final Completion
- **1 John 3:2–3**: "When Christ appears, we shall be like him."
- **Romans 8:29–30**: Predestined "to be conformed to the image of his Son."

## Struggle in the Process
- **Romans 7:14–25**: Paul's description of inner conflict with sin.
- **Philippians 3:12–14**: "Not that I have already... been made perfect, but I press on."

Christian traditions understand these passages somewhat differently. Reformed, Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox views differ on topics like entire sanctification, theosis, and how sanctification relates to justification. If you're interested in a particular tradition's reading, I'd be glad to go deeper.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the means of grace?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 10:17, Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 28:19
questions.response:
# Scripture and the Means of Grace

The phrase "means of grace" doesn't appear in the Bible. It is a theological term for the instruments through which God gives His grace, forgiveness, and faith. Christian traditions draw on a common set of passages, though they interpret and count the means somewhat differently.

## 1. The Word of God
Most Protestant traditions treat the Word, read and especially preached, as the primary means.
- **Romans 10:14–17**: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ."
- **Isaiah 55:10–11**: God's word "shall not return to me empty."
- **1 Peter 1:23–25**: Born again "through the living and abiding word of God."
- **James 1:18**: "He brought us forth by the word of truth."
- **2 Timothy 3:15–17**: Scripture makes one "wise for salvation."
- **Hebrews 4:12**: The word is "living and active."
- **1 Thessalonians 2:13**: The word "is at work in you believers."
- **John 17:17**: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth."

## 2. Baptism
- **Matthew 28:18–20**: The command to baptize all nations.
- **Mark 16:16**: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved."
- **John 3:5**: Born "of water and the Spirit."
- **Acts 2:38–39**: "Be baptized… for the forgiveness of your sins… for the promise is for you and for your children."
- **Acts 22:16**: "Be baptized and wash away your sins."
- **Romans 6:3–4**: Baptized into Christ's death and resurrection.
- **Galatians 3:27**: "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
- **Colossians 2:11–12**: Baptism as the circumcision made without hands.
- **Titus 3:5**: "The washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit."
- **Ephesians 5:25–26**: Cleansing "by the washing of water with the word."
- **1 Peter 3:21**: "Baptism… now saves you."

## 3. The Lord's Supper
- **Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24; Luke 22:19–20**: The words of institution, including "for the forgiveness of sins" (Matthew).
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17**: The cup and bread as a "participation" (*koinonia*) in Christ's blood and body.
- **1 Corinthians 11:23–29**: Paul's account, with warnings about unworthy eating.
- **John 6:48–58**: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life." Whether this refers directly to the Supper is debated.

## 4. Absolution / Confession (especially Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox)
- **John 20:21–23**: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them."
- **Matthew 16:19; 18:18**: The keys of binding and loosing.
- **James 5:14–16**: "Confess your sins to one another."

## 5. Prayer and Other Practices (Reformed and Methodist emphases)
The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 88) names the Word, sacraments, and prayer. John Wesley also included fasting, Scripture searching, and Christian fellowship ("Christian conference").
- **Acts 2:42**: Devoted "to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers." This is often cited as a summary text.
- **Matthew 7:7–11; Philippians 4:6–7; James 1:5**: On prayer.
- **Hebrews 10:24–25**: Not neglecting to meet together.
- **Matthew 6:16–18**: On fasting.

## How Traditions Differ
- **Lutheran**: Word and Sacraments (Baptism, Supper, often Absolution) truly deliver forgiveness and create and strengthen faith.
- **Reformed/Presbyterian**: Word, sacraments, and prayer, made effective by the Spirit for the elect. The sacraments are signs and seals of the covenant.
- **Methodist**: "Instituted" means (prayer, Scripture, Supper, fasting, fellowship) and "prudential" means.
- **Catholic/Orthodox**: The seven sacraments (mysteries) as the chief channels of grace, alongside Scripture and prayer.
- **Baptist and many evangelicals**: Usually prefer "ordinances" to "sacraments," seeing Baptism and the Supper mainly as acts of obedience and remembrance, with the Word and prayer central

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
# Key Bible Passages Cited in Support of Covenant Theology

Covenant theology, associated especially with Reformed and Presbyterian traditions, organizes Scripture around three overarching covenants: the **covenant of redemption**, the **covenant of works**, and the **covenant of grace**. Below are the passages most commonly cited for each element.

---

## 1. The Covenant of Redemption (Pactum Salutis)
*An eternal agreement within the Trinity in which the Father appoints the Son to redeem the elect.*

- **John 6:37–40**: The Father gives a people to the Son, who will lose none of them.
- **John 17:2–6, 24**: Jesus speaks of those the Father "gave me" and the work the Father gave Him to do.
- **Ephesians 1:3–11**: Election "in Christ before the foundation of the world."
- **Psalm 110**: The Father's oath to the Son as King and Priest.
- **Isaiah 53:10–12**: The Servant's reward for His suffering.
- **Titus 1:2; 2 Timothy 1:9**: Grace and promise given "before the ages began."
- **Luke 22:29**: "As my Father covenanted to me a kingdom" (the Greek verb *diatithemai* is related to *diathēkē*, "covenant").

## 2. The Covenant of Works
*God's arrangement with Adam, promising life for obedience and death for disobedience.*

- **Genesis 2:16–17**: The command and the threatened penalty.
- **Hosea 6:7**: "Like Adam they transgressed the covenant" (the translation is debated; some render it "like men" or as a place name).
- **Romans 5:12–21**: Adam and Christ as two representative heads.
- **1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49**: The "first Adam" and the "last Adam."
- **Leviticus 18:5; Galatians 3:10–12; Romans 10:5**: The principle "do this and live."

## 3. The Covenant of Grace
*God's gracious covenant, after the fall, to save sinners through Christ, administered progressively through the biblical covenants.*

**First announcement**
- **Genesis 3:15**: The *protoevangelium*, the promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent.

**Noahic Covenant**
- **Genesis 6:18; 8:20–9:17**: God's preserving covenant that sustains the stage for redemption.

**Abrahamic Covenant**, central to the system
- **Genesis 12:1–3; 15; 17:1–14**: Promise of land, seed, and blessing to the nations. "I will be your God and the God of your offspring after you" (17:7).
- **Galatians 3:6–9, 14, 16–18, 29**: Believers in Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs. The law, coming 430 years later, does not annul the promise.
- **Romans 4**: Abraham as father of all who believe, circumcised and uncircumcised.

**Mosaic Covenant**
- **Exodus 19–24**: Given to a redeemed people (Exod. 20:2), which covenant theologians read as grace preceding law.
- **Galatians 3:19–24**: The law as a guardian leading to Christ.

**Davidic Covenant**
- **2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89; Psalm 132**: An everlasting throne, fulfilled in Christ (**Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:29–36**).

**New Covenant**
- **Jeremiah 31:31–34**: The law written on hearts and sins forgiven.
- **Ezekiel 36:25–27**: A new heart and the Spirit.
- **Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25**: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood."
- **Hebrews 8–10**: Christ as mediator of a better covenant, fulfilling earlier shadows.
- **2 Corinthians 3**: The ministry of the new covenant.

## 4. Unity and Continuity of God's People
*A distinctive emphasis: one people of God across both Testaments.*

- **Romans 11:16–24**: One olive tree, with Gentiles grafted in.
- **Ephesians 2:11–22**: Gentiles brought into "the covenants of promise," making one new man.
- **Galatians 6:16**: "The Israel of God."
- **1 Peter 2:9–10**: Israel's titles (Exod. 19:5–6) applied to the church.
- **Hebrews 11**: Old Testament saints saved by faith, looking forward to Christ.
- **Acts 7:38**: Israel called the "congregation" (*ekklēsia*) in the wilderness.

## 5. Covenant Signs and Households
*Used by paedobaptist covenant theologians to support infant baptism.*

- **Genesis 17:7–14**: Covenant sign given to children.
- **Colossians 2:11–12**: Circumcision and baptism linked.
- **Acts 2:38–39**: "The promise is for you and for your children."
- **Acts 16:15, 31–34; 1 Corinthians 1:16**: Household baptisms.
- **1 Corinthians 7:14**: Children of a believer are "holy."

## 6. The Recurring Covenant Formula
The refrain "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" runs through Scripture and is seen as evidence of one unfolding covenant purpose:
**Genesis 17:7; Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Hebrews 8:10; Revelation 21:3**

---

## Points of Debate
- **Dispensationalists

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
# The Lord's Supper in the Bible

## The Institution Accounts (the Last Supper)
Jesus established the meal on the night before his crucifixion, during the Passover:
- **Matthew 26:26–29**: "Take, eat; this is my body… this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."
- **Mark 14:22–25**: A parallel account, closely similar to Matthew.
- **Luke 22:14–20**: Includes the command "Do this in remembrance of me" and calls the cup "the new covenant in my blood."

## Paul's Teaching
- **1 Corinthians 11:17–34**: The most detailed instruction. Paul uses the phrase "the Lord's Supper" (v. 20), repeats the words of institution (vv. 23–26), says the meal "proclaims the Lord's death until he comes," and warns against taking it "in an unworthy manner," urging self-examination (vv. 27–32).
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17**: Describes the cup and bread as a "participation" (Greek *koinonia*, communion) in Christ's blood and body, and stresses the unity of believers: "we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread."
- **1 Corinthians 10:21**: Contrasts the "table of the Lord" with pagan sacrificial meals.

## Practice in the Early Church
- **Acts 2:42, 46**: Believers devoted themselves to "the breaking of bread" and prayer.
- **Acts 20:7, 11**: The church in Troas gathered "on the first day of the week… to break bread."

## Related Passages
- **John 6:22–59**: Jesus' "Bread of Life" discourse ("Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life"). Christians debate whether this refers directly to the Supper or more broadly to faith in Christ.
- **John 13–17**: John's account of the Last Supper, which focuses on foot-washing and Jesus' farewell teaching rather than the bread and cup.
- **Luke 24:30–35**: The risen Jesus is recognized "in the breaking of the bread" at Emmaus.

## Old Testament Background
- **Exodus 12**: The Passover meal, the setting of the Last Supper, commemorating deliverance from Egypt.
- **Exodus 24:8**: "The blood of the covenant," echoed in Jesus' words.
- **Jeremiah 31:31–34**: The promise of a "new covenant," which Jesus says is inaugurated in his blood.

## A Note on Interpretation
Christian traditions read these texts differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches teach a real change or real presence. Lutherans hold to a sacramental union. Reformed churches speak of a spiritual presence. Many Baptist and other traditions emphasize a memorial view. All of them, however, draw on these same core passages.

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
Here are the main biblical passages on baptism, grouped by theme.

## Old Testament Background and Foreshadowing
- **Genesis 6–9**: The flood, later linked to baptism in 1 Peter 3:20–21
- **Exodus 14**: Crossing the Red Sea, called a "baptism into Moses" in 1 Corinthians 10:1–2
- **Ezekiel 36:25–27**: "I will sprinkle clean water on you…" (cleansing and the new heart/Spirit)
- **Genesis 17**: Circumcision as covenant sign, connected to baptism in Colossians 2:11–12

## John the Baptist's Baptism
- **Matthew 3:1–12; Mark 1:4–8; Luke 3:1–18; John 1:19–34**: A baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins, pointing to Christ who baptizes "with the Holy Spirit and fire"
- **Acts 19:1–7**: Disciples of John rebaptized in Jesus' name

## The Baptism of Jesus
- **Matthew 3:13–17; Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22**: Jesus is baptized "to fulfill all righteousness," and the Trinity is revealed

## Institution and Command
- **Matthew 28:18–20**: The Great Commission: "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"
- **Mark 16:15–16**: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved" (note: this is in the longer ending of Mark, which has textual questions)
- **John 3:5**: "Born of water and the Spirit" (whether this refers to baptism is debated)
- **John 3:22–23; 4:1–2**: Jesus' disciples baptizing

## Baptism in the Early Church (Acts)
- **Acts 2:38–41**: "Repent and be baptized… for the forgiveness of your sins"
- **Acts 8:12–17**: Samaritans baptized
- **Acts 8:36–39**: The Ethiopian eunuch ("went down into the water")
- **Acts 9:18; 22:16**: Paul's baptism ("wash away your sins, calling on his name")
- **Acts 10:44–48**: Cornelius's household, baptized after receiving the Spirit
- **Acts 16:14–15, 31–34**: Household baptisms of Lydia and the Philippian jailer
- **Acts 18:8**: Crispus and many Corinthians

## Theological Meaning (Epistles)
- **Romans 6:1–11**: Baptized into Christ's death and resurrection; newness of life
- **1 Corinthians 1:13–17**: Paul on baptizing and divisions
- **1 Corinthians 12:13**: "By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body"
- **1 Corinthians 15:29**: Baptism "for the dead" (a notoriously difficult verse)
- **Galatians 3:26–29**: "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ"
- **Ephesians 4:4–6**: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism"
- **Ephesians 5:25–27**: "The washing of water with the word"
- **Colossians 2:11–12**: "Buried with him in baptism," linked to circumcision
- **Titus 3:5**: "The washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit"
- **Hebrews 6:1–2**: "Instruction about washings/baptisms" as a foundational teaching
- **Hebrews 10:22**: "Bodies washed with pure water"
- **1 Peter 3:18–22**: "Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you… as an appeal to God for a good conscience"

## Related Uses of "Baptism"
- **Mark 10:38–39; Luke 12:50**: Jesus' suffering described as a "baptism"
- **Acts 1:5; 11:16**: Baptism with the Holy Spirit

## Key Debated Issues and Relevant Texts
| Issue | Commonly Cited Passages |
|---|---|
| **Subjects** (believers only vs. infants too) | Acts 2:38–39; 16:15, 33; 1 Cor 1:16; Col 2:11–12; Mark 10:13–16 |
| **Mode** (immersion, pouring, sprinkling) | Mark 1:10; Acts 8:38–39; Rom 6:4; Ezek 36:25; Acts 2:17 |
| **Efficacy** (sacrament/means of grace vs. symbol/ordinance) | Acts 2:38; 22:16; Titus 3:5; 1 Pet 3:21; Rom 6:3–4 |
| **Formula** (Trinitarian vs. "in Jesus' name") | Matt 28:19; Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5 |

If you're studying this from a particular tradition (Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist, Orthodox, etc.), I can point you to how that tradition interprets these passages or to its key confessional documents.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
The New Testament contains a good deal of material on church leadership, though Christians have long disagreed about how to put it together. Here are the main passages.

## Key Passages on Elders/Overseers

**Qualifications**
- **1 Timothy 3:1–7**: Qualifications for overseers (*episkopos*)
- **Titus 1:5–9**: Paul instructs Titus to "appoint elders in every town" and lists qualifications
- **1 Peter 5:1–4**: Peter, a "fellow elder," exhorts elders to shepherd the flock willingly and by example

**Function and Authority**
- **Acts 20:17–35**: Paul addresses the Ephesian elders, calling them overseers who "shepherd the church of God" (v. 28)
- **1 Timothy 5:17–22**: Elders who "rule well" deserve double honor; guidelines for accusations against elders
- **Hebrews 13:7, 17**: Believers are to obey and submit to their leaders, who "keep watch over your souls"
- **1 Thessalonians 5:12–13**: Respect those who "are over you in the Lord"
- **James 5:14**: Elders pray for and anoint the sick

**Appointment**
- **Acts 14:23**: Paul and Barnabas appointed elders "in every church"
- **Acts 6:1–6**: The congregation selects the Seven, and the apostles appoint them (often seen as a model for deacons)

## Deacons
- **1 Timothy 3:8–13**: Qualifications for deacons
- **Philippians 1:1**: Paul greets "the overseers and deacons"
- **Romans 16:1**: Phoebe, described as a *diakonos* of the church at Cenchreae

## Broader Church Order
- **Acts 15**: The Jerusalem Council, where apostles and elders deliberate together, often cited for multi-church authority
- **Matthew 18:15–20** and **1 Corinthians 5**: Church discipline involving the gathered congregation
- **Ephesians 4:11–13**: Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers to equip the saints
- **1 Corinthians 12** and **Romans 12**: The church as a body with diverse gifts

## Old Testament Background
- **Exodus 18** and **Numbers 11:16–25**: Moses appoints elders and leaders to share the burden of governing Israel

## Points of Interpretation

Christians draw different conclusions from these texts:

- **Episcopal** (Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist): Bishops hold distinct authority. Supporters point to Timothy and Titus as apostolic delegates, and Catholic and Orthodox traditions also appeal to apostolic succession and early church practice (e.g., Ignatius of Antioch).
- **Presbyterian/Reformed**: Churches are governed by a plurality of elders, with higher courts (presbyteries and synods). Supporters often cite Acts 15.
- **Congregational** (many Baptists, independents): The congregation holds final authority, often led by elders and deacons. Supporters cite Matthew 18 and Acts 6.

Recurring questions include whether "elder" (*presbyteros*) and "overseer" (*episkopos*) are the same office (Acts 20:17, 28 and Titus 1:5–7 use them interchangeably), whether there is a distinction between teaching and ruling elders (based on 1 Tim 5:17), and debates about women's roles in leadership (1 Tim 2:12, Rom 16).

For further reading, the book *Who Runs the Church? 4 Views on Church Government* (Zondervan) presents the major positions side by side.

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
# Bible Passages on the Second Coming of Christ

## Old Testament Foreshadowing
- **Daniel 7:13–14**: The "Son of Man" coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom (a passage Jesus later applies to himself).
- **Zechariah 12:10; 14:3–5**: The Lord standing on the Mount of Olives and the people looking on "the one they have pierced."

## Jesus' Own Teaching
- **Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 21:25–36**: The Olivet Discourse, describing signs, the Son of Man coming "on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory," and the command to watch.
- **Matthew 24:36–44**: No one knows the day or hour; the coming will be like the days of Noah.
- **Matthew 25**: Parables of the ten virgins and the talents, and the judgment of the sheep and goats (25:31–46).
- **Matthew 16:27; 26:64**: The Son of Man coming in glory with his angels.
- **Luke 17:22–37**: The coming will be sudden and visible, like lightning.
- **John 14:1–3**: "I will come back and take you to be with me."

## Acts
- **Acts 1:9–11**: The angels say Jesus "will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven."
- **Acts 3:19–21**: Heaven must receive Christ until the time to restore everything.

## Paul's Letters
- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18**: The Lord descends with a shout; the dead in Christ rise and believers are "caught up" to meet him.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:1–11**: The day of the Lord comes "like a thief in the night."
- **2 Thessalonians 1:6–10; 2:1–12**: Christ revealed from heaven in blazing fire; events preceding his coming.
- **1 Corinthians 15:20–28, 50–58**: Resurrection at his coming; the dead raised "in the twinkling of an eye."
- **Philippians 3:20–21**: Awaiting a Savior who will transform our bodies.
- **Colossians 3:4**: "When Christ… appears, then you also will appear with him in glory."
- **Titus 2:13**: "The blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior."
- **1 Corinthians 11:26**: The Lord's Supper proclaims his death "until he comes."

## Other New Testament Letters
- **Hebrews 9:28**: Christ will appear a second time to bring salvation.
- **James 5:7–8**: Be patient, for the Lord's coming is near.
- **2 Peter 3:3–13**: Answering scoffers; God's timing and the new heavens and new earth.
- **1 John 2:28; 3:2–3**: When he appears, we shall be like him.
- **Jude 14–15**: The Lord coming with his holy ones to judge.

## Revelation
- **Revelation 1:7**: "Every eye will see him."
- **Revelation 19:11–16**: Christ returning on a white horse as King of kings.
- **Revelation 20–22**: The millennium, final judgment, and new creation.
- **Revelation 22:7, 12, 20**: "I am coming soon." / "Come, Lord Jesus."

## Recurring Themes
1. **Certainty**: Christ will return.
2. **Visibility**: It will be personal, bodily, and public.
3. **Unknown timing**: No one knows the day (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7).
4. **Resurrection and judgment** accompany his return.
5. **Readiness**: Believers are called to watchfulness, holiness, and hope.

**Note:** Christians interpret details differently, such as the timing of the "rapture," the millennium, and how much of the Olivet Discourse was fulfilled in AD 70. Major views include premillennialism, amillennialism, postmillennialism, and preterism. If you're interested, I can explain any of these perspectives.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the final judgment?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 25:31-46, Rev 20:11-15, 2 Cor 5:10, Acts 17:31
questions.response:
The final judgment appears throughout Scripture, from the Old Testament prophets to the New Testament. Here are the key passages, grouped by theme.

## Old Testament

- **Ecclesiastes 12:14**: "For God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil."
- **Daniel 7:9–10**: A vision of the Ancient of Days on his throne, with "the court seated, and the books opened."
- **Daniel 12:2**: "Multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake: some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt." This is one of the clearest Old Testament references to resurrection and judgment.
- **Psalm 96:13 and 98:9**: The Lord "comes to judge the earth... in righteousness."
- **Isaiah 66:15–16, 22–24**: Judgment by fire and the new heavens and new earth.
- **Joel 3:12–16**: The nations gathered in the "Valley of Jehoshaphat" for judgment.
- **Malachi 3:1–5; 4:1–3**: The coming "day of the Lord."

## The Gospels

- **Matthew 25:31–46**: The sheep and the goats. Christ, seated on his throne, separates the nations and judges them by how they treated "the least of these."
- **Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43, 47–50**: The parables of the wheat and weeds and of the net, which describe separation "at the end of the age."
- **Matthew 12:36–37**: People will give account for "every careless word."
- **John 5:22–29**: The Father has given all judgment to the Son. All in the graves will come out, "those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
- **John 3:17–19 and 12:48**: Judgment tied to the response to Christ and his word.

## The Epistles

- **Romans 2:5–16**: The "day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed," when God "will repay each person according to what they have done" and judge "people's secrets through Jesus Christ."
- **Romans 14:10–12**: "We will all stand before God's judgment seat."
- **2 Corinthians 5:10**: "We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ."
- **1 Corinthians 3:12–15**: Believers' works tested by fire.
- **Acts 17:30–31**: Paul in Athens says God "has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed."
- **2 Thessalonians 1:5–10**: Judgment at Christ's return.
- **Hebrews 9:27**: "People are destined to die once, and after that to face judgment."
- **2 Peter 3:7–13**: The present heavens and earth "reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment."
- **Jude 14–15**: The Lord coming "to judge everyone."

## Revelation

- **Revelation 20:11–15**: The fullest picture, the **Great White Throne judgment**. The dead, great and small, stand before God. Books are opened, including "the book of life," and people are judged "according to what they had done."
- **Revelation 21–22**: What follows: the new heaven and new earth, and the final separation of the redeemed from the unrepentant.

## Recurring Themes

1. **Universality**: All people, living and dead, will be judged.
2. **Christ as Judge**: The Father has entrusted judgment to the Son.
3. **Judgment according to works**: Deeds, words, and even secrets are revealed.
4. **Grace and faith**: Passages like John 3:18, John 5:24, and Romans 8:1 teach that those in Christ do not face condemnation.
5. **Final outcomes**: Eternal life or eternal separation, followed by the renewal of creation.

Christian traditions differ on some details, such as whether there is one judgment or several and how it relates to the millennium, but nearly all affirm a future, final judgment by Christ. If you'd like, I can go deeper into a particular passage or explain how different traditions interpret these texts.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about heaven and hell?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rev 21:1-4, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, John 14:2-3
questions.response:
# Scripture Passages on Heaven and Hell

The Bible's teaching on the afterlife develops across both Testaments. Below are key passages, grouped by theme, with brief notes.

---

## Old Testament Background

The Hebrew Scriptures say less about the afterlife than the New Testament does, and they often speak of **Sheol**, the shadowy realm of the dead.

- **Psalm 16:10–11** – "You will not abandon me to Sheol... in your presence there is fullness of joy."
- **Psalm 49:15** – "God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol."
- **Job 19:25–27** – "I know that my Redeemer lives... in my flesh I shall see God."
- **Isaiah 25:8** – God "will swallow up death forever" and wipe away tears.
- **Isaiah 65:17; 66:22–24** – New heavens and new earth, with a closing image of judgment ("their worm shall not die").
- **Daniel 12:2** – "Many who sleep in the dust... shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." This is the clearest Old Testament statement of a two-fold resurrection.

---

## Heaven / Eternal Life

**Jesus' teaching**
- **John 14:1–3** – "In my Father's house are many rooms... I go to prepare a place for you."
- **John 3:16; 5:24; 11:25–26** – Eternal life through belief in Christ.
- **Matthew 5:3–12** – The Beatitudes promise the kingdom of heaven.
- **Matthew 25:34** – "Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."
- **Luke 23:43** – To the thief on the cross: "Today you will be with me in paradise."

**Paul's letters**
- **1 Corinthians 2:9** – "What no eye has seen... God has prepared for those who love him."
- **1 Corinthians 15** – The resurrection of the body; death defeated (vv. 42–57).
- **2 Corinthians 5:1–8** – "Away from the body and at home with the Lord."
- **Philippians 1:21–23** – "To depart and be with Christ, which is far better."
- **Philippians 3:20–21** – "Our citizenship is in heaven"; bodies transformed.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18** – The dead in Christ rise; "we will always be with the Lord."

**Other New Testament writings**
- **Hebrews 11:16; 12:22–24** – A heavenly city, the heavenly Jerusalem.
- **1 Peter 1:3–5** – An inheritance "imperishable, undefiled, and unfading."
- **Revelation 7:9–17** – A multitude from every nation before the throne.
- **Revelation 21–22** – New heaven and new earth: God dwells with his people, there is no more death or pain, and the tree of life appears.

---

## Hell / Judgment

Several terms are used: **Sheol** (Hebrew, the grave or realm of the dead), **Hades** (Greek equivalent), **Gehenna** (the valley of Hinnom, used by Jesus as an image of final judgment), and the **lake of fire**.

**Jesus' teaching**
- **Matthew 5:22, 29–30** – Warnings about Gehenna.
- **Matthew 10:28** – "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell."
- **Matthew 13:41–42, 49–50** – "The furnace of fire... weeping and gnashing of teeth."
- **Matthew 25:41, 46** – "Eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels... eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life."
- **Mark 9:43–48** – "Unquenchable fire... where their worm does not die."
- **Luke 16:19–31** – The rich man and Lazarus in Hades. Interpreters debate whether this is a parable or a literal description.

**Other New Testament writings**
- **Romans 2:5–8** – Wrath and righteous judgment according to deeds.
- **2 Thessalonians 1:8–9** – "Eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord."
- **Hebrews 9:27** – "It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment."
- **2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6–7** – Judgment of fallen angels; Sodom as an example of "eternal fire."
- **Revelation 14:10–11** – "The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever."
- **Revelation 20:10–15** – The final judgment before the great white throne; death and Hades thrown into the lake of fire, "the second death."

---

## Interpretive Perspectives

Christians read these texts in different ways:

- **Eternal conscious punishment** is the traditional majority view, emphasizing Matthew 25:46 and Revelation 14 and 20.
- **Conditional immortality (annihilationism)** holds that the wicked are ultimately destroyed, citing language of "destruction" and "perishing" (Matthew 10:28; John 3:16; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).
- **Christian universalism** is a minority view that hopes all will ultimately be reconciled, drawing on passages such as 1 Corinthians 15:22, Colossians 1:20, and 1 Timothy 2:4.
- **Purgatory**, held in Catholic teaching, is a purification after death for those saved, drawing on 1 Corinthians 3:12–15 and tradition, including 2 Maccabees 12.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of creation?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 1:1, John 1:3, Col 1:16, Heb 11:3
questions.response:
# Where the Bible Teaches the Doctrine of Creation

The doctrine of creation runs throughout Scripture, not just in its opening chapters.

## 1. The Foundational Accounts
- **Genesis 1:1–2:3**: God creates the heavens and the earth by His word over six days, declares creation "good," and rests on the seventh day.
- **Genesis 2:4–25**: A complementary account focused on the formation of humanity, the garden, and the creation of man and woman.

## 2. Poetry and Wisdom Literature
- **Psalm 8**: Humanity's place and dignity in creation.
- **Psalm 19:1–6**: "The heavens declare the glory of God."
- **Psalm 33:6–9**: "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made... he spoke, and it came to be."
- **Psalm 90:2**: God existed before the mountains and the world.
- **Psalm 104**: An extended hymn on God's creating and sustaining work.
- **Psalms 136:5–9 and 148:5**: Creation as grounds for praise.
- **Job 38–41**: God's speeches from the whirlwind ("Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?").
- **Proverbs 3:19–20; 8:22–31**: God created by wisdom, which is personified as present at creation.

## 3. The Prophets
- **Isaiah 40:12–28**: The incomparable Creator who measures the waters and names the stars.
- **Isaiah 42:5; 44:24; 45:7, 12, 18**: God alone stretched out the heavens and formed the earth "to be inhabited."
- **Jeremiah 10:12; 32:17**: Creation as evidence of God's power.
- **Amos 4:13; 5:8**: The Creator as the Lord of hosts.
- **Nehemiah 9:6**: "You alone are the LORD... you made the heavens."

## 4. The New Testament
- **John 1:1–3**: "All things were made through him" (the Word, Christ).
- **Colossians 1:15–17**: All things were created in, through, and for Christ, and in Him "all things hold together."
- **Hebrews 1:2–3**: The Son is the agent of creation and sustains all things.
- **Hebrews 11:3**: The universe was formed by God's word, "so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible."
- **Romans 1:20**: God's power and nature are evident in creation.
- **Romans 4:17**: God "calls into existence the things that do not exist."
- **Acts 14:15; 17:24–28**: Paul preaches God as Creator to pagan audiences.
- **1 Corinthians 8:6**: One God "from whom are all things" and one Lord "through whom are all things."
- **Matthew 19:4 / Mark 10:6**: Jesus appeals to the creation of male and female.
- **Revelation 4:11**: "You created all things, and by your will they existed."

## 5. Key Themes and Their Supporting Texts

| Theme | Key Passages |
|---|---|
| Creation out of nothing (*ex nihilo*) | Gen 1:1; Rom 4:17; Heb 11:3; also 2 Maccabees 7:28 in Catholic and Orthodox canons |
| Trinitarian involvement | Gen 1:2, 26; Ps 33:6; Ps 104:30; John 1:3; Col 1:16 |
| Goodness of creation | Gen 1:31; 1 Tim 4:4 |
| Humanity in God's image | Gen 1:26–27; 9:6; Ps 8; James 3:9 |
| God's ongoing sustaining (providence) | Ps 104; Neh 9:6; Col 1:17; Heb 1:3 |
| Creation's fall and hope | Gen 3; Rom 8:19–22 |
| New creation | Isa 65:17; 66:22; 2 Cor 5:17; 2 Pet 3:13; Rev 21–22 |

## A Note on Interpretation
Christians broadly agree that God is the sole, sovereign Creator of all things. They differ, however, on *how* to read Genesis 1–2.
