questions.question: What passages teach about God's providence?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 10:29-31, Rom 8:28, Eph 1:11, Dan 4:35
questions.response:
# Bible Passages on God's Providence

Providence is the teaching that God sustains creation and guides events toward his purposes. Here are key passages, grouped by theme.

## God Sustains All Creation
- **Psalm 104:10–30**: God waters the earth, feeds animals, and gives breath to all living things.
- **Colossians 1:16–17**: "In him all things hold together."
- **Hebrews 1:3**: The Son "upholds the universe by the word of his power."
- **Acts 17:24–28**: "In him we live and move and have our being."
- **Nehemiah 9:6**: "You preserve all of them."

## God Cares for the Smallest Details
- **Matthew 6:25–34**: The birds of the air and lilies of the field; "do not be anxious."
- **Matthew 10:29–31**: Not a sparrow falls apart from the Father; every hair is numbered.
- **Psalm 145:15–16**: "You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing."
- **Proverbs 16:33**: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD."

## God Governs Human Affairs and Nations
- **Proverbs 16:9**: "The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps."
- **Proverbs 21:1**: The king's heart is like streams of water in the LORD's hand.
- **Daniel 2:21; 4:34–35**: God removes and sets up kings; none can stay his hand.
- **Isaiah 46:9–10**: "My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose."
- **Ephesians 1:11**: God "works all things according to the counsel of his will."

## God Brings Good Out of Evil and Suffering
- **Genesis 50:20**: Joseph to his brothers: "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good."
- **Romans 8:28**: "For those who love God all things work together for good."
- **Acts 2:23; 4:27–28**: The crucifixion, carried out by wicked hands, fulfilled God's plan.
- **2 Corinthians 4:17**: Light momentary affliction prepares an eternal weight of glory.

## Providence in Narrative Form
- **The story of Joseph (Genesis 37–50)**: Betrayal and slavery lead to the preservation of many lives.
- **The Book of Esther**: God is never named, yet "coincidences" deliver his people (see 4:14, "for such a time as this").
- **The Book of Ruth**: An apparently chance encounter in Boaz's field (2:3) leads to the line of David.
- **1 Kings 17**: Elijah fed by ravens and by the widow of Zarephath.

## Personal Guidance and Comfort
- **Psalm 23**: The Lord as shepherd who provides, leads, and protects.
- **Psalm 139:13–16**: God's knowledge of us before birth; all our days are written in his book.
- **Jeremiah 29:11**: "Plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope." (Originally addressed to the exiles in Babylon.)
- **Philippians 4:19**: "My God will supply every need of yours."
- **Lamentations 3:22–23, 37–38**: His mercies are new every morning, and nothing happens unless the Lord has commanded it.

## Providence and Human Responsibility
- **Philippians 2:12–13**: "Work out your own salvation… for it is God who works in you."
- **James 4:13–15**: "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that."

---

**For further study:** The *Heidelberg Catechism* (Q&A 27–28) and the *Westminster Confession* (Chapter 5) offer classic summaries of the doctrine. Theologians also differ on how providence relates to human free will (Calvinist, Arminian, and Molinist views, for example), so these passages are often read in different ways.

Would you like me to expand on any of these themes?

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the nature and practice of prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Phil 4:6, 1 Thess 5:17, John 14:13-14
questions.response:
Scripture addresses prayer throughout, both through direct teaching and through recorded examples. Here are the major passages, grouped by theme.

## Jesus' Direct Teaching
- **Matthew 6:5–15**: The Lord's Prayer, with warnings against praying for show or using "empty phrases." Includes the call to pray in secret and the link between receiving and extending forgiveness.
- **Luke 11:1–13**: The disciples ask, "Lord, teach us to pray." Jesus gives the prayer, then the parable of the persistent friend at midnight and "ask, seek, knock."
- **Luke 18:1–8**: The persistent widow and the unjust judge, told so that people "ought always to pray and not lose heart."
- **Luke 18:9–14**: The Pharisee and the tax collector, contrasting self-righteousness with humble repentance.
- **Matthew 7:7–11**: God as a good Father who gives good gifts.
- **John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24**: Praying in Jesus' name.
- **Mark 11:22–25**: Faith and forgiveness in prayer.
- **Matthew 18:19–20**: Agreement in corporate prayer.

## Jesus' Own Prayer Life
- **Mark 1:35; Luke 5:16; 6:12**: He withdrew to solitary places to pray, sometimes all night.
- **John 17**: The "High Priestly Prayer" for His disciples and future believers.
- **Matthew 26:36–46**: Gethsemane, "not as I will, but as you will," a model of surrender.

## Apostolic Teaching
- **Philippians 4:6–7**: Prayer with thanksgiving in place of anxiety, and the peace of God that follows.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:16–18**: "Pray without ceasing."
- **Romans 8:26–27**: The Spirit intercedes for us when we don't know how to pray.
- **Ephesians 6:18**: Praying at all times in the Spirit, for all the saints.
- **1 Timothy 2:1–8**: Prayers for all people, including rulers.
- **James 5:13–18**: Prayer in suffering and sickness, confession, and "the prayer of a righteous person has great power" (with Elijah as the example).
- **James 1:5–8; 4:2–3**: Asking in faith, and asking with wrong motives.
- **1 John 5:14–15**: Confidence in praying according to God's will.
- **Hebrews 4:14–16**: Approaching the throne of grace with confidence through Christ.
- **Colossians 4:2**: Devotion, watchfulness, and thanksgiving.

## Old Testament Foundations
- **The Psalms**: Israel's prayer book, covering the full range of prayer: lament (Ps 13, 22, 88), confession (Ps 51), praise (Ps 103, 145), trust (Ps 23, 62), and longing (Ps 42, 63).
- **Genesis 18:22–33**: Abraham intercedes for Sodom.
- **Exodus 32:11–14; 33:12–23**: Moses intercedes for Israel.
- **1 Samuel 1–2**: Hannah's anguished prayer and song of thanksgiving.
- **1 Kings 8**: Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication.
- **2 Chronicles 7:14**: Humility, prayer, and turning from sin.
- **Daniel 6, 9**: Daniel's habitual prayer and his prayer of corporate confession.
- **Nehemiah 1**: Confession and petition.
- **Jeremiah 29:12–13**: "You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart."
- **Habakkuk**: Honest wrestling with God, ending in trust (3:17–19).

## Prayer in the Early Church
- **Acts 1:14; 2:42; 4:23–31; 12:5; 13:1–3**: The early church devoted itself to corporate prayer.
- **Paul's prayers**: Ephesians 1:15–23 and 3:14–21, Philippians 1:9–11, and Colossians 1:9–14 are rich models of intercession.

## Themes That Emerge
Taken together, these passages present prayer as:
- **Relational**: addressing God as Father
- **Humble and honest**: including lament and confession
- **Persistent and faithful**
- **Aligned with God's will**
- **Mediated through Christ and aided by the Spirit**
- **Both private and communal**
- **Accompanied by thanksgiving**

For a starting point, Matthew 6, Luke 11, and a handful of Psalms give a strong foundation. If you'd like, I can suggest a reading plan or go deeper on any particular aspect, such as unanswered prayer, fasting, or intercession.

questions.question: Where are the Ten Commandments given in Scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:1-17, Deut 5:6-21
questions.response:
The Ten Commandments appear in two main places in the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament):

1. **Exodus 20:1–17.** God speaks the commandments to Israel at Mount Sinai, shortly after the exodus from Egypt.
2. **Deuteronomy 5:6–21.** Moses repeats the commandments to the next generation on the plains of Moab before they enter the Promised Land.

The two versions are nearly identical, with a few notable differences:
- **Sabbath command:** Exodus grounds it in God resting after creation (Exod 20:11). Deuteronomy grounds it in Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt (Deut 5:15).
- **Coveting command:** Exodus lists the neighbor's "house" first, then his wife. Deuteronomy lists the wife first and adds "his field."

**Related passages:**
- **Exodus 31:18 and 32:15–19** describe the two stone tablets "written with the finger of God" and Moses breaking them.
- **Exodus 34:1–28** describes the replacement tablets. Verse 28 uses the phrase "the ten words" (Hebrew *aseret ha-devarim*), the source of the term "Decalogue." This is also echoed in Deuteronomy 4:13 and 10:4.

**Numbering:** The text doesn't number the commandments explicitly, so traditions divide them differently:
- **Jewish tradition** treats "I am the LORD your God…" as the first statement.
- **Catholic and Lutheran traditions** combine the prohibitions on other gods and idols and split the coveting command into two.
- **Most Protestant and Orthodox traditions** separate other gods and idols into two commandments and keep coveting as one.

In the New Testament, Jesus and Paul cite several of the commandments, for example in Matthew 19:18–19, Mark 10:19, and Romans 13:9.

questions.question: Where does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Luke 11:2-4
questions.response:
The Lord's Prayer appears in two places in the New Testament, in two different settings.

**1. Matthew 6:9–13, the Sermon on the Mount**
Jesus teaches the prayer as part of his longer Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), delivered on a mountainside in Galilee. It comes within a section on sincere religious practice, where Jesus warns against praying showily or with "empty phrases" like the pagans, and then says, "Pray then like this…" This is the longer version, and it is the basis for the form most commonly used in churches today.

**2. Luke 11:2–4, in response to a request**
Here the setting is different. Jesus is praying "in a certain place," and when he finishes, one of his disciples asks, "Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples." Jesus responds with a shorter version of the prayer, followed by the parable of the persistent friend at midnight and teaching about asking, seeking, and knocking. In Luke's narrative this occurs during Jesus' journey toward Jerusalem.

**Traditional location**
Christian tradition associates Luke's account with the **Mount of Olives** near Jerusalem. The **Church of the Pater Noster** stands there today, and its walls display the prayer in more than 100 languages.

**A note on the ending**
The familiar closing doxology, "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen," is not found in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew or Luke. It appears in some later manuscripts and in the early Christian text the *Didache*, and it was likely added for liturgical use.

questions.question: What passages address the sacraments in Reformed theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4
questions.response:
# Key Passages on the Sacraments in Reformed Theology

## Scripture Passages

**Sacraments generally (sign and seal)**
- **Genesis 17:1–14**: Circumcision as the covenant sign
- **Romans 4:11**: Circumcision as "a sign... a seal of the righteousness of faith," which is foundational to Reformed sacramental language
- **Exodus 12**: The Passover, seen as an Old Testament parallel to the Supper
- **1 Corinthians 10:1–4**: Israel's "baptism" and spiritual food and drink, showing continuity between the testaments

**Baptism**
- **Matthew 28:18–20**: The institution of baptism
- **Romans 6:3–4** and **Colossians 2:11–12**: Union with Christ, and baptism linked to circumcision
- **Acts 2:38–39**: "The promise is for you and your children," a key text for infant baptism
- **Acts 16:15, 33** and **1 Corinthians 1:16**: Household baptisms
- **1 Corinthians 7:14**: Children of believers called "holy"
- **Titus 3:5**, **1 Peter 3:21**, **Galatians 3:27**, **Ephesians 5:26**

**The Lord's Supper**
- **Matthew 26:26–29**, **Mark 14:22–25**, **Luke 22:14–20**: The institution
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17**: The "participation" (koinonia) in Christ's body and blood, central to Calvin's view of spiritual presence
- **1 Corinthians 11:23–32**: Proper administration and self-examination before taking the Supper
- **John 6:47–58**: Feeding on Christ, a debated text that Reformed writers apply to faith-union with Christ more broadly

## Confessional and Theological Texts

| Source | Sections |
|---|---|
| **Calvin, *Institutes*** | Book IV, chs. 14–19 (sacraments, baptism, infant baptism, Supper, the Mass, false sacraments) |

| **Westminster Larger Catechism** | Q&A 161–177 |
| **Westminster Shorter Catechism** | Q&A 91–97 |
| **Heidelberg Catechism** | Q&A 65–82 (Q&A 80 addresses the Mass) |
| **Belgic Confession** | Articles 33–35 |
| **Second Helvetic Confession** | Chs. 19–21 |
| **Scots Confession** | Chs. 21–23 |

## Further Theological Reading
- Francis Turretin, *Institutes of Elenctic Theology*, Topic 19
- Herman Bavinck, *Reformed Dogmatics*, vol. 4
- Louis Berkhof, *Systematic Theology*, Part 5
- Heinrich Heppe, *Reformed Dogmatics* (a compilation of older sources)

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about church discipline?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 18:15-17, 1 Cor 5:1-13, Titus 3:10, 2 Thess 3:14-15
questions.response:
The New Testament addresses church discipline in several key passages, and the Old Testament provides some background.

## Primary Passages

**Matthew 18:15–20.** Jesus gives the foundational process:
1. Go to the person privately.
2. If they don't listen, take one or two others as witnesses.
3. If they still refuse, tell it to the church.
4. If they refuse to listen even to the church, treat them "as a Gentile and a tax collector."

The passage also includes the "binding and loosing" authority and the promise of Christ's presence "where two or three are gathered."

**1 Corinthians 5.** Paul rebukes the Corinthian church for tolerating a man in an incestuous relationship. He instructs them to "deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved" (v. 5), warns that "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (v. 6), and concludes, "Purge the evil person from among you" (v. 13). He also clarifies that this applies to those inside the church, not outsiders (vv. 9–12).

**2 Corinthians 2:5–11.** This passage, often linked to 1 Corinthians 5, urges the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love for a repentant offender so he isn't "overwhelmed by excessive sorrow." It shows that restoration is the goal.

## Supporting Passages

- **Galatians 6:1.** Restore a person caught in sin "in a spirit of gentleness," watching yourself.
- **2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15.** Keep away from the idle and disobedient, yet "do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother."
- **Romans 16:17–18.** Watch out for and avoid those who cause divisions contrary to sound teaching.
- **Titus 3:10–11.** Warn a divisive person once, then twice, and then have nothing more to do with them.
- **1 Timothy 1:19–20.** Paul handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan "that they may learn not to blaspheme."
- **1 Timothy 5:19–20.** Accusations against elders require two or three witnesses, and persistent sinners are rebuked publicly.
- **James 5:19–20.** Whoever brings back a wanderer "will save his soul from death."
- **Jude 22–23.** Show mercy to doubters and snatch others from the fire.
- **Revelation 2:14–16, 20.** Christ rebukes churches in Pergamum and Thyatira for tolerating false teaching and immorality.

## Old Testament Background

- **Deuteronomy 19:15.** The two-or-three-witnesses principle, which Jesus and Paul cite.
- **Deuteronomy 13, 17, 22.** The repeated phrase "purge the evil from your midst," which Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 5:13.
- **Leviticus 19:17.** "You shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him."

## Recurring Themes

These passages consistently emphasize:
- **Restoration** of the sinner (Gal 6:1; 2 Cor 2; James 5)
- **Purity** of the church (1 Cor 5)
- **Protection** of others from harm or false teaching (Titus 3; Rom 16)
- **Humility and gentleness** in those who correct
- **Due process**, through witnesses and gradual steps

Christian traditions differ on how to apply these texts, for example on who exercises discipline (congregation, elders, or bishops), what offenses warrant it, and what exclusion looks like in practice. Many of these debates arise from interpreting the passages above.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about Christian liberty?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gal 5:1, 1 Cor 8:9, Rom 14:1-23, 1 Pet 2:16
questions.response:
Christian liberty is a significant theme in the New Testament, especially in Paul's letters. Here are the key passages, grouped by aspect.

## 1. Freedom from Sin's Bondage
- **John 8:31–36**: "If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." Jesus contrasts slavery to sin with the freedom He gives.
- **Romans 6:6–7, 14–18, 22**: Believers are "set free from sin" and become "slaves of righteousness."
- **Romans 8:1–2**: "The law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death."

## 2. Freedom from the Law's Condemnation and Ceremonial Requirements
- **Galatians 5:1**: "For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery." This is perhaps the central text.
- **Galatians 2:4–5**: Paul resists "false brothers" who sought to spy out "our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus."
- **Galatians 3:13, 23–25; 4:1–7**: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, and believers are no longer under a guardian but are sons and heirs.
- **Colossians 2:16–23**: "Let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath." Human regulations ("Do not handle, do not taste") are rejected.
- **Acts 15:1–29**: The Jerusalem Council declines to impose circumcision and the Mosaic law on Gentile believers ("a yoke… that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear," v. 10).

## 3. Liberty of Conscience in Disputable Matters
- **Romans 14:1–15:7**: The fullest treatment. It covers foods and special days ("One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind," 14:5). Believers should not despise or judge one another, and "whatever does not proceed from faith is sin" (14:23).
- **1 Corinthians 8**: Food offered to idols. Knowledge "puffs up," but love builds up, so believers should take care that their liberty does not become a stumbling block to the weak.
- **1 Corinthians 10:23–33**: "All things are lawful, but not all things are helpful." Do all to the glory of God and seek the good of others.
- **1 Timothy 4:1–5**: Forbidding marriage and foods is condemned, because "everything created by God is good… if it is received with thanksgiving."

## 4. Freedom from Human Traditions Binding the Conscience
- **Matthew 15:1–20 / Mark 7:1–23**: Jesus rebukes those who "teach as doctrines the commandments of men."
- **1 Corinthians 7:23**: "You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men."
- **James 4:12**: "There is only one lawgiver and judge."

## 5. The Limits and Purpose of Liberty
- **Galatians 5:13–14**: "Do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another."
- **1 Peter 2:16**: "Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God."
- **1 Corinthians 6:12**: "'All things are lawful for me,' but I will not be dominated by anything."
- **1 Corinthians 9:19–23**: Paul, though free, makes himself a servant to all to win more people.
- **Romans 6:1–2, 15**: Grace is not a license to sin.
- **Jude 4**: Warning against those who "pervert the grace of our God into sensuality."

## 6. Freedom Through the Spirit and the Gospel
- **2 Corinthians 3:17**: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom."
- **James 1:25; 2:12**: "The perfect law, the law of liberty."
- **Luke 4:18**: Jesus proclaims "liberty to the captives" (citing Isaiah 61:1).
- **Hebrews 9:14; 10:22**: Consciences cleansed by Christ's blood.

## Summary of the Biblical Teaching
1. Christ frees believers from the guilt and dominion of sin and from the condemnation of the law.
2. Believers are not bound by Old Testament ceremonial regulations or by human rules that go beyond Scripture.
3. In matters Scripture does not command or forbid, believers may act according to conscience without judging others.
4. Liberty is governed by love: it should not be used to harm a weaker brother or sister, to indulge the flesh, or to excuse sin.
5. True freedom is not autonomy but freedom *for* serving God and neighbor.

## For Further Study
- Martin Luther, *The Freedom of a Christian* (1520): "A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all."
- John Calvin, *Institutes* 3.19
- Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 20, "Of Christian Liberty, and Liberty of Conscience"

Galatians and Romans 14 make an excellent starting point for in-depth study.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 2:24, Eph 5:22-33, Matt 19:4-6, Heb 13:4
questions.response:
The Bible addresses marriage in many places. Here are the most significant passages, grouped by theme:

## Foundations in Creation
- **Genesis 1:27–28**: God creates humanity male and female and blesses them.
- **Genesis 2:18–25**: "It is not good for the man to be alone." Woman is created as a suitable partner, and "a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh" (2:24).

## Teachings of Jesus
- **Matthew 19:3–12** (also **Mark 10:2–12**): Jesus quotes Genesis, affirms the permanence of marriage ("what God has joined together, let no one separate"), and discusses divorce and celibacy.
- **Matthew 5:27–32**: Teaching on adultery, lust, and divorce in the Sermon on the Mount.
- **Matthew 22:23–30**: Marriage in relation to the resurrection.
- **John 2:1–11**: Jesus performs his first miracle at a wedding in Cana.

## Paul's Letters
- **Ephesians 5:21–33**: The fullest New Testament passage. It calls for mutual submission, asks husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, and describes marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
- **1 Corinthians 7**: An extended discussion of marriage, singleness, sexual relations within marriage, divorce, and marrying believers or unbelievers.
- **Colossians 3:18–19**: Brief instructions to wives and husbands.
- **1 Timothy 3:2, 12** and **Titus 1:6**: Marriage qualifications for church leaders.
- **1 Timothy 4:1–5**: Paul condemns those who forbid marriage.

## Other New Testament Passages
- **Hebrews 13:4**: "Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure."
- **1 Peter 3:1–7**: Instructions to wives and husbands, including that husbands should be considerate and treat their wives with respect as "co-heirs of the gracious gift of life."

## Wisdom Literature
- **Proverbs 5:15–20**: Faithfulness and delight in one's spouse.
- **Proverbs 18:22**: "He who finds a wife finds what is good."
- **Proverbs 31:10–31**: Portrait of a capable, honorable wife.
- **Ecclesiastes 9:9**: Enjoy life with the spouse you love.
- **Song of Songs**: A poetic celebration of romantic and physical love.

## Law and Prophets
- **Exodus 20:14**: "You shall not commit adultery."
- **Deuteronomy 24:1–5**: Laws on divorce and newlyweds.
- **Malachi 2:13–16**: God as witness to the marriage covenant, with a strong statement against faithless divorce.
- **Hosea 1–3**: Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife illustrates God's faithful love for Israel.

## Narratives
- **Genesis 24**: Isaac and Rebekah.
- **Genesis 29**: Jacob, Leah, and Rachel.
- **Ruth**: The story of Ruth and Boaz.

## Marriage as a Spiritual Metaphor
- **Isaiah 54:5; 62:4–5**, **Jeremiah 2:2**, and **Ezekiel 16**: God as husband to his people.
- **Revelation 19:7–9; 21:2**: The "wedding supper of the Lamb," with the church as the bride of Christ.

If you're studying a particular aspect, such as roles, divorce, or singleness, I can go deeper into those passages and how different Christian traditions interpret them.

questions.question: What passages address the role of the civil magistrate?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 13:1-7, 1 Pet 2:13-17, Acts 5:29, Dan 2:21
questions.response:
The phrase "civil magistrate" is used mostly in Reformation and Puritan theology. Below are the main biblical passages, grouped by theme, followed by the confessional and theological texts that treat the topic most directly.

## Biblical Passages

**Divine origin of civil authority**
- **Romans 13:1–7**: The central text. Authorities are "instituted by God," the ruler is "God's servant for your good," he "does not bear the sword in vain," and taxes and honor are owed.
- **Proverbs 8:15–16**: "By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just."
- **Daniel 2:21; 4:17, 25, 32**: God "removes kings and sets up kings."
- **John 19:11**: Jesus tells Pilate, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above."

**Purpose: punishing evil and promoting good**
- **Genesis 9:5–6**: The foundation of judicial authority over the shedding of blood.
- **1 Peter 2:13–17**: Governors are sent "to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good." "Honor the emperor."
- **1 Timothy 2:1–4**: Christians pray for kings "that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way."

**Qualifications and duties of rulers**
- **Exodus 18:21–22**: Rulers should be "able men… who fear God, are trustworthy and hate a bribe."
- **Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 16:18–20**: Judges must judge impartially and pursue justice.
- **Deuteronomy 17:14–20**: The law of the king, who must not exalt himself and must keep God's law.
- **2 Samuel 23:3–4**: "When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God…"
- **2 Chronicles 19:5–7**: Jehoshaphat tells his judges, "You judge not for man but for the LORD."
- **Psalm 82**: Rulers must defend the weak, the fatherless, and the poor.
- **Proverbs 16:12; 20:26, 28; 29:4, 14**: Wisdom sayings on righteous kingship.
- **Psalm 2:10–12**: "Be wise, O kings… Kiss the Son."

**Christians' duties toward rulers**
- **Matthew 22:15–22 / Mark 12:13–17 / Luke 20:20–26**: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
- **Titus 3:1**: "Be submissive to rulers and authorities."
- **Jeremiah 29:7**: "Seek the welfare of the city… pray to the LORD on its behalf."

**Limits of civil authority and lawful disobedience**
- **Acts 4:19–20; 5:29**: "We must obey God rather than men."
- **Exodus 1:15–21**: The Hebrew midwives defy Pharaoh.
- **Daniel 3 and 6**: Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego, and Daniel refuse idolatrous commands.
- **1 Samuel 8**: Samuel warns of the abuses of kings.
- **Revelation 13

questions.response:
# A Reformed Evaluation of Election Based on Foreseen Faith

**Verdict:** Reformed theology rejects this statement. It describes *conditional election*, the position associated with Jacobus Arminius and the Remonstrants, which the Synod of Dort (1618–19) explicitly repudiated. The Reformed position is **unconditional election**: God chooses individuals to salvation according to His sovereign good pleasure, not because of anything foreseen in them, including faith.

---

## 1. Confessional Witness

The Reformed confessions address this view directly:

- **Westminster Confession of Faith 3.5:** God chose the elect "out of His mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith, or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving Him thereunto."
- **Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 9:** "This election was not made on the basis of foreseen faith, the obedience of faith, holiness, or any other good quality... as a prerequisite, cause, or condition... but rather for the purpose of faith, holiness, and so on."
- **Canons of Dort, Rejection of Errors 1.5:** It explicitly rejects the teaching that "foreseen faith... is the cause or condition on which God's election is based."

The key Reformed reversal: faith is not the *ground* of election but its *fruit*. God does not elect people because they will believe; they believe because they are elect.

---

## 2. Exegetical Arguments

### Romans 8:29, the meaning of "foreknew"
The statement leans on this verse: "For those whom he foreknew he also predestined..." Reformed interpreters argue:

- The Greek *proginōskō* reflects the Hebrew *yada*, which often means covenantal, personal knowing, an intimate setting of affection on someone (Gen 18:19; Jer 1:5; Amos 3:2; Matt 7:23, where Jesus "never knew" people whose existence He obviously knew about).
- The object of foreknowledge is *persons* ("those whom"), not their faith or actions.
- In the "golden chain" (8:29–30), God is the sole actor at every link. Nothing in the text introduces human faith as the deciding factor.
- Compare Romans 11:2: "God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew," which means those He set His love upon, not those whose choices He predicted.

### Romans 9:11–16
Paul's argument seems designed to exclude conditional election: Jacob was chosen "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls." He concludes: "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy" (9:16). Reformed exegetes note that if election rested on foreseen faith, the objection Paul anticipates ("Is there injustice on God's part?" v. 14) would never arise.

### Other key texts
- **Ephesians 1:4–5, 11:** Election is "according to the purpose of his will" and "the counsel of his will," and is unto holiness, not on account of it.
- **Acts 13:48:** "As many as were appointed to eternal life believed." Appointment precedes and produces faith.
- **John 6:37, 44, 65:** Coming to Christ is the result of the Father's giving and drawing.
- **John 15:16:** "You did not choose me, but I chose you."

---

## 3. Theological Arguments

**a. Total depravity makes foreseen faith impossible.** If fallen humans are "dead in trespasses and sins" (Eph 2:1) and unable to come to Christ unless drawn (John 6:44), then left to themselves there is no faith for God to foresee. The only faith God could foresee is faith He Himself grants.

**b. Faith is God's gift.** Ephesians 2:8–9, Philippians 1:29, and Acts 13:48 and 16:14 present faith as something given. If God gives faith, He cannot coherently base His choice on foreseeing it. That would be circular: God elects those who believe, but they believe only because He gives faith, which He gives to those He elects.

**c. It relocates the decisive factor in the human.** If two people hear the same gospel with the same grace and one believes, conditional election implies that the ultimate difference lies in the person. Reformed theologians argue this reintroduces grounds for boasting (1 Cor 4:7: "What do you have that you did not receive?").

**d. It inverts the order of God's decree.** Reformed theology holds that God's knowledge of what *will* happen rests on His decree of what *shall* happen. God doesn't "look down the corridor of time" at an independently determined future; the future is certain because He has ordained it (Isa 46:10; Eph 1:11).

**e. It makes grace contingent.** Election becomes God's response to human merit-like qualities, undermining *sola gratia*.

---

## 4. Fair Representation of the Opposing View

Arminian and Wesleyan theologians would respond that:
- *Foreknowledge* in 1 Peter 1:1–2 and Romans 8:29 naturally means prior knowledge.
- Prevenient grace enables all people to believe, so faith is still grace-enabled and not meritorious.
- Romans 9 concerns corporate or national election (Israel and the Gentiles) to

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free will of man."
questions.reference_answer: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose

required_points: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted
God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of resistible grace. Should affirm irresistible (effectual) grace.

questions.response:
# A Reformed Evaluation

From a Reformed perspective, this statement would be judged **false**. It essentially restates the third article of the Remonstrance (1610), which the Synod of Dort (1618–19) rejected. Reformed theology does not hold that humans never resist God. It holds that God's *saving* grace, when He purposes to save, cannot be *ultimately* or *finally* resisted.

## 1. The Key Distinction: Outward Call vs. Effectual Call

Reformed theology distinguishes two ways God calls people:

- **The general (outward) call:** the preaching of the gospel to all, inviting everyone to repent and believe. This call *can* be and often is resisted. Reformed theologians readily affirm Acts 7:51 ("You always resist the Holy Spirit").
- **The effectual (inward) call:** the Spirit's work in the elect by which He regenerates the heart and brings the person to faith. This call is *invariably effective*.

So the Reformed tradition affirms that grace in its general operations is resisted daily, but denies that God's saving purpose toward His elect can be finally thwarted.

The Westminster Confession (10.1) describes effectual calling as God "taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by His almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ: yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace."

## 2. The Problem with "Free Will" in the Statement

The statement assumes that the unregenerate will is free to accept or reject grace. Reformed theology, following Augustine and Luther's *The Bondage of the Will*, rejects this premise:

- **Total depravity (inability):** Fallen humans are "dead in trespasses and sins" (Eph. 2:1). The will is not destroyed, but it is enslaved to sin and freely, willingly chooses against God (Rom. 8:7–8; John 6:44).
- **Freedom properly defined:** Humans act according to their strongest desires and nature. The unregenerate are "free" only to choose sin. They are not coerced, but neither are they neutral.

The Reformed would therefore say the statement misplaces the problem. The issue is not that grace is too weak to overcome the will. Without grace, the will never wants God in the first place.

## 3. Regeneration Precedes Faith

Reformed theology holds that regeneration logically precedes faith. God does not merely offer assistance that the sinner may accept or decline. He gives new life, out of which faith flows. The Canons of Dort (III/IV.12) describe regeneration as:

> "an entirely supernatural work, one that is at the same time most powerful and most pleasing, a marvelous, hidden, and inexpressible work, which is not lesser than or inferior in power to that of creation or of raising the dead."

Just as a corpse cannot resist resurrection, a spiritually dead sinner cannot finally resist the Spirit's life-giving work.

## 4. Key Scriptural Arguments

- **John 6:37, 44:** "All that the Father gives me *will* come to me… No one can come to me unless the Father… draws him." Those drawn are raised up at the last day, so the drawing is effective.
- **Romans 8:29–30:** The "golden chain": those predestined are called, those called are justified, those justified are glorified. No one drops out between links.
- **Ezekiel 36:26–27:** "I will give you a new heart… and *cause* you to walk in my statutes."
- **Philippians 2:13:** God works in believers "both to will and to work for his good pleasure."
- **John 1:13:** Believers are born "not of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **Acts 16:14:** "The Lord opened [Lydia's] heart to pay attention."

## 5. Theological Concerns with the Statement

Reformed theologians would raise several objections:

1. **God's sovereignty:** If saving grace can be finally resisted, God's purposes in salvation depend ultimately on human decision, which contradicts texts like Isaiah 46:10 and Ephesians 1:11.
2. **Grounds for boasting:** If two people receive equal grace and one accepts while the other resists, the difference lies in the individual. This seems to undermine Ephesians 2:8–9 and 1 Corinthians 4:7 ("What do you have that you did not receive?").
3. **Assurance and perseverance:** If grace can be resisted at the outset, it is unclear why it could not also be resisted afterward. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance depends on grace being effectual.
4. **The unity of the Trinity's work:** The Father elects, the Son redeems, and the Spirit applies. A resistible application would make the Spirit's work potentially fail where the Father and Son have purposed salvation.

## 6. Clarifying Misunderstandings

Reformed theologians typically add several caveats:

# Evaluating "A Truly Regenerate Believer Can Lose Their Salvation": A Reformed Assessment

## The Verdict

From a Reformed perspective, this statement is **false**. Reformed theology holds to the **perseverance of the saints** (the "P" in TULIP): those whom God has truly regenerated and united to Christ will be kept by God's power and will persevere in faith to the end. They may stumble seriously, but they cannot *totally* or *finally* fall away.

## Confessional Basis

The major Reformed confessions address this directly:

- **Westminster Confession of Faith 17.1:** "They whom God hath accepted in His Beloved, effectually called, and sanctified by His Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved."
- **Canons of Dort, Fifth Head of Doctrine:** Written specifically against the Remonstrants (Arminians), it affirms that God "does not wholly withdraw the Holy Spirit from his own people, even in their melancholy falls."
- **Heidelberg Catechism Q&A 1:** Christ "so preserves me that without the will of my heavenly Father not a hair can fall from my head."

## The Theological Grounds

Reformed theology rests perseverance on God's work, not on the believer's strength. WCF 17.2 says it depends "not upon their own free will, but upon the immutability of the decree of election." The grounds include:

1. **The unchangeable decree of election.** God's purpose in predestination does not fail (Romans 8:29–30). The "golden chain" moves unbroken from foreknowledge to glorification. No one drops out between justification and glory.

2. **The finished work and ongoing intercession of Christ.** Christ's atonement secures salvation for those for whom it was made, and He "always lives to make intercession for them" (Hebrews 7:25; cf. John 17:11–12, 24; Luke 22:32).

3. **The sealing and indwelling of the Holy Spirit.** The Spirit is the "guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30). A guarantee that could be revoked would guarantee nothing.

4. **The nature of the new covenant.** God promises, "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40). In the new covenant God secures the faithfulness of His people as well as His own.

5. **The nature of regeneration itself.** New birth is a sovereign act of God creating a new nature (John 3:3–8; 1 John 3:9). Reformed theologians argue it cannot be "undone," just as physical birth cannot be.

6. **Union with Christ.** Believers are in Christ, and nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38–39).

## Key Supporting Texts

- **John 6:37–40:** "All that the Father gives me will come to me... that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
- **John 10:27–29:** "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand."
- **Philippians 1:6:** "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ."
- **1 Peter 1:5:** Believers are those "who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed."
- **1 John 2:19:** "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us."

Reformed theology does not simply teach "once saved, always saved" in a popular, careless sense. Several nuances matter:

**1. Believers can fall seriously, though not finally.**
WCF 17.3 acknowledges that believers may "fall into grievous sins, and for a time continue therein," incurring God's displeasure, grieving the Spirit, losing comfort and assurance, hardening their hearts, and bringing temporal judgments on themselves. David and Peter are the classic examples. Their falls were real and grievous, but they were restored.

# A Reformed Evaluation of the Statement

**"Christ died equally for every individual person, intending to save all without distinction."**

## Summary Verdict

Reformed theology rejects this statement. It closely matches the second article of the Remonstrance (1610), the Arminian position the Synod of Dort (1618–19) answered directly. The Reformed doctrine is called **definite atonement** or **particular redemption**: Christ died with the specific intention of securing the salvation of the elect, and his death actually accomplishes that salvation.

The Reformed response is more nuanced than a simple denial, however. It is worth separating the statement's claims.

---

## 1. Breaking Down the Statement

| Element | Reformed Response |
|---|---|
| "Christ died..." | Affirmed: a real, substitutionary, penal atonement |
| "...for every individual person" | Qualified: the death is *sufficient* for all but *efficient* for the elect |
| "...equally" | Denied: Christ's death bears a special relation to the elect that it does not bear to others |
| "...intending to save all" | Denied: God's saving intention in the cross is coextensive with election |
| "...without distinction" | Partly affirmed in one sense: Christ saves people "of every tribe and tongue" (Rev 5:9), without ethnic or social distinction, but not every individual without exception |

---

## 2. Confessional Basis

**Canons of Dort, Second Head, Article 8:**
> "For this was the sovereign counsel and most gracious will and purpose of God the Father, that the quickening and saving efficacy of the most precious death of his Son should extend to all the elect... that is, it was the will of God that Christ by the blood of the cross... should effectually redeem out of every people, tribe, nation, and language, all those, and those only, who were from eternity chosen to salvation."

**Westminster Confession 8.5:**
> Christ "purchased not only reconciliation, but an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him."

**Westminster Confession 3.6:**
> "Neither are any other redeemed by Christ... but the elect only."

---

## 3. The Main Reformed Arguments

### a) The unity of the Trinity's saving purpose
The Father elects, the Son redeems, and the Spirit applies redemption. If the Son died to save all while the Father chose only some and the Spirit regenerates only some, the persons of the Godhead would be working toward different ends.
- John 6:37–39: "All that the Father gives me will come to me... that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me."
- Ephesians 1:3–14 presents election, redemption, and sealing as one coordinated work.

### b) The efficacy of the atonement
Scripture describes the cross as *accomplishing* salvation, not merely making it possible:
- "He will save his people from their sins" (Matt 1:21)
- "Having obtained eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12)
- "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb 10:14)

If Christ intended to save all equally, and not all are saved, then his intention failed. On this view the decisive factor in salvation becomes the human response rather than the cross itself.

### c) The "double payment" argument (John Owen)
In *The Death of Death in the Death of Christ* (1647), Owen argued that Christ bore the punishment either for:
1. all the sins of all people,
2. some sins of all people, or
3. all the sins of some people.

If (1), why are any punished? If one says "because of unbelief," is unbelief not a sin for which Christ died? Owen concluded that (3) alone is coherent with penal substitution. (Critics, including some Reformed theologians, consider this argument too commercial in its logic, but it remains influential.)

### d) Particular language in Scripture
- Christ lays down his life "for the sheep" (John 10:11, 15), and some are "not of my sheep" (10:26).
- "Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Eph 5:25).
- "The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood" (Acts 20:28).

# A Reformed Evaluation of Universal Prevenient Grace

The statement is a fair summary of the Wesleyan-Arminian position. Reformed theology would **reject it as stated**, though it would affirm some of the concerns behind it. Here is how a Reformed theologian would likely analyze it.

---

## 1. Points of Partial Agreement

Reformed theology shares some ground with the doctrine:

- **Grace must come first.** Both traditions reject Pelagianism and semi-Pelagianism. Fallen humans cannot initiate their own salvation. Arminius and Wesley both affirmed total depravity, which is why they needed prevenient grace in the first place.
- **God gives grace to all people.** Reformed theology teaches *common grace*: God restrains sin, gives rain on the just and unjust (Matt. 5:45), and preserves civic virtue and culture. But common grace is non-saving. It does not restore the ability to believe.
- **The gospel offer is sincere and universal.** Reformed preaching calls all people to repent and believe (Acts 17:30), and the Canons of Dort affirm that the call is "seriously" made to all (III/IV.8).

So the disagreement is not about whether grace precedes faith. It is about **what kind of grace, given to whom, with what effect.**

---

## 2. Main Objections

### a. The Nature of Spiritual Inability
Reformed theology holds that the fallen will is not merely weakened but **dead** toward God (Eph. 2:1–5; Rom. 8:7–8). The remedy Scripture describes is not *enablement* but *resurrection* and *new birth* (John 3:3–8; Ezek. 36:26). A dead person is not restored to neutrality, then left to choose life. He is made alive.

> "All mankind... are by nature children of wrath, incapable of any saving good... and without the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, they are neither able nor willing to return to God." — *Canons of Dort* III/IV.3

### b. The Lack of Explicit Biblical Basis
Reformed critics argue that universal prevenient grace is a theological inference rather than a clearly taught doctrine. Texts often cited, such as John 1:9 ("the true light, which gives light to everyone") and John 12:32 ("I will draw all people to myself"), are read differently:
- John 1:9 is taken to refer to general revelation, or to Christ coming into the world as the light available to all kinds of people.
- John 12:32's "all" is read in context (Greeks had just sought Jesus, 12:20–21) as "all kinds of people," not every individual.

### c. John 6 and Effectual Drawing
John 6:44 states: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, **and I will raise him up** on the last day." Reformed exegetes note that the one drawn is the one raised. The drawing is therefore effective, not merely enabling. John 6:37 ("All that the Father gives me will come to me") and 6:65 reinforce that coming to Christ is a sovereign gift.

### d. The Ultimate Differentiating Factor
If all receive the same enabling grace, then what finally distinguishes the believer from the unbeliever is the person's own choice. Reformed theology sees this as compromising 1 Corinthians 4:7 ("What do you have that you did not receive?") and opening room for boasting (Eph. 2:8–9). In the Reformed view, faith itself is God's gift, and the believer owes even the decision to believe to grace.

> "Faith is therefore to be considered as the gift of God, not on account of its being offered by God to man, to be accepted or rejected at his pleasure; but because it is in reality conferred, breathed, and infused into him." — *Canons of Dort* III/IV.14

### e. The Unity of the Divine Will in Salvation
Romans 8:29–30 presents an unbroken chain: those predestined are called, justified, and glorified. Reformed theology argues that the saving call here cannot be a universal, resistible grace, since all who receive it are glorified. This "effectual calling" (WCF 10.1) is particular and certain.

### f. Freedom Redefined
The statement assumes freedom means the *power of contrary choice* (libertarian freedom). Most Reformed theologians hold a *compatibilist* view: a person is free when acting according to their desires without external coercion. Regeneration does not violate freedom. It renews the desires so the person comes "most freely, being made willing by his grace" (WCF 10.1).

---

## 3. The Reformed Alternative

| Universal Prevenient Grace (Arminian) | Reformed View |
|---|---|
| Given to all | Common grace to all; saving grace to the elect |
| Restores ability to choose | Regenerates the heart, producing faith |
| Resistible | Effectual (often called "irresistible") |
| Faith precedes regeneration | Regeneration precedes faith (logically) |
| Human choice is the decisive factor | God's sovereign mercy is decisive |

---

## 4. Fairness to the Other Side

A responsible Reformed evaluation should acknowledge the strongest Arminian replies:
- Texts like 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9 express God's desire for all to be saved. Reformed theologians address these through distinctions in God's will (decretive vs. preceptive) or by reading "all" contextually, but they admit these are serious texts.
- Arminians argue the Reformed view makes God the author of reprobation or renders the universal offer insincere. # A Reformed Evaluation of Libertarian Free Will

## The Verdict

Reformed theology **rejects** this statement. It objects to two distinct claims within it:

1. That fallen man can **choose between good and evil** (a claim about moral ability)
2. That this choice occurs **apart from God's determining will** (a claim about divine sovereignty)

Reformed theology does not deny that humans make real, voluntary, responsible choices. It denies that those choices are *libertarian* in the sense described.

---

## 1. What Reformed Theology Affirms About the Will

The Westminster Confession (9.1) states:

> "God hath endued the will of man with that natural liberty, that it is neither forced, nor by any absolute necessity of nature determined to good or evil."

So the Reformed tradition affirms:
- **Natural liberty**: humans choose according to their own desires, without external coercion.
- **Genuine agency**: people are not puppets. They act willingly and are accountable.
- **Secondary causes**: God's decree does not eliminate creaturely causation but *establishes* it (WCF 3.1: "nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established").

The disagreement is therefore about the *nature and condition* of freedom, not whether it exists.

---

## 2. First Problem: Moral Inability After the Fall

Following Augustine, Reformed theology describes the will across the **fourfold state of man** (WCF 9.2–5; Boston, *Human Nature in Its Fourfold State*):

| State | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Innocence** (Adam before the fall) | Able to sin and able not to sin (*posse peccare, posse non peccare*) |
| **Fallen** (unregenerate) | Not able not to sin (*non posse non peccare*) |
| **Regenerate** | Able not to sin, though still sinning (*posse non peccare*) |
| **Glorified** | Not able to sin (*non posse peccare*) |

WCF 9.3 states plainly:

> "Man, by his fall into a state of sin, hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation... so as a natural man, being altogether averse from that good, and dead in sin, is not able, by his own strength, to convert himself, or to prepare himself thereunto."

**Key texts:**
- **Romans 8:7–8**: the mind set on the flesh "does not submit to God's law; indeed, it *cannot*."
- **John 6:44**: "No one *can* come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."
- **Ephesians 2:1–5**: the unregenerate are "dead in trespasses and sins."
- **John 8:34**: "Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
- **Jeremiah 13:23**: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin...? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil."

The fallen person is free to do what he wants, but he does not want God. Luther's *The Bondage of the Will* (1525), written against Erasmus, and the Canons of Dort (Heads III/IV) make the same point. The will is not neutral between good and evil. It is enslaved to sin until renewed by grace.

**Edwards' distinction** (*Freedom of the Will*, 1754) is helpful here:
- **Natural ability**: the person has the faculties needed to obey (mind, will, body). This grounds responsibility.
- **Moral inability**: the person lacks the *disposition* to obey. This is culpable, not an excuse.

A man who cannot repent because he hates God is not thereby innocent. His inability *is* his sin.

---

## 3. Second Problem: "Apart From God's Determining Will"

WCF 3.1 states:

> "God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass."

**Key texts on divine sovereignty over human choices:**
- **Ephesians 1:11**: God "works all things according to the counsel of his will."
- **Proverbs 21:1**: "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will."
- **Proverbs 16:9**: "The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps."
- **Genesis 50:20**: "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good."
- **Acts 2:23; 4:27–28**: the crucifixion was carried out by "lawless men" yet according to "the definite plan and foreknowledge of God."

Acts 2:23 is especially important. The most evil act in history was both fully *predetermined* by God and fully *culpable* for those who did it. Scripture holds both together without apology.

From a Reformed view, a human choice "apart from God's determining will" would mean:
- Something in creation escapes God's providence (contrary to Matthew 10:29–30)
- God's foreknowledge depends on the creature, making God dependent
- God's purposes could be frustrated (contrary to Isaiah 46:10; Daniel 4:35)

---

## The Statement in Context

The statement paraphrases the dogmatic constitution *Pastor Aeternus* of the First Vatican Council (1870), which declared that when the Roman Pontiff speaks *ex cathedra*, defining doctrine on faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he possesses the infallibility Christ willed for His Church, and that such definitions are "irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church" (*ex sese, non autem ex consensu Ecclesiae*).

The Reformed tradition rejects this claim. Its objections are not merely anti-Roman sentiment. They follow from its doctrines of Scripture, the Church, and Christ's headship.

The central Reformed objection is that infallibility belongs to Scripture alone as the Word of God.

- **Belgic Confession, Art. 7:** "We may not consider any writings of men, however holy these men may have been, of equal value with the divine Scriptures... for all men are of themselves liars."

From this view, papal infallibility creates a second infallible authority alongside Scripture, one that in practice governs how Scripture may be read. The Reformed would say this inverts the proper relationship: the Church is created by the Word (*creatura verbi*), not the Word's master.

The Reformed do not deny that the Church has real authority, but they define it as **ministerial and declarative**, not **magisterial and legislative**.

- **WCF 31.4:** "All synods or councils, since the apostles' times, whether general or particular, may err; and many have erred. Therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith, or practice; but to be used as a help in both."

If ecumenical councils, which Rome itself honors, can err, then a single bishop has no greater claim to inerrancy. The Reformed hold their own confessions as *subordinate standards* (*norma normata*), always reformable by Scripture (*norma normans*). The phrase "irreformable" therefore strikes at the heart of the Reformation principle *ecclesia semper reformanda*: the Church must always be reformed by the Word of God.

- **The "rock" of Matthew 16:18:** Many Reformed interpreters, following strands of patristic exegesis including some of Augustine's readings, identify the rock as Peter's confession

# A Reformed Evaluation

**Verdict:** From a Reformed perspective, the statement is **incorrect**. It describes something real in the Christian life, but it assigns it to the wrong category. Inner renewal belongs to *sanctification*. Justification is a *forensic declaration* based on the *imputed* righteousness of Christ, not an infused righteousness inherent in the believer.

---

## 1. What the Statement Gets Wrong

### Justification is declarative, not transformative
In Reformed theology, justification is a legal (forensic) act of God as Judge. He pronounces the sinner righteous; he does not make the sinner righteous within. The Westminster Confession states this directly:

> "Those whom God effectually calleth, He also freely justifieth; **not by infusing righteousness into them**, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone..." (WCF 11.1)

The Confession seems almost written against the statement in question, and historically it was. The phrase "not by infusing righteousness" deliberately rejects the Council of Trent, which taught that the "single formal cause" of justification is the righteousness of God "by which He makes us just," infused into the soul (Session 6, ch. 7; cf. Canon 11).

### The righteousness is alien, not inherent
Following Luther, the Reformers spoke of *iustitia aliena*, an "alien" or external righteousness. The believer stands before God clothed in Christ's obedience, not in a quality residing in himself. The Heidelberg Catechism puts it this way:

> "Even though my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments... God, **without any merit of my own**, out of mere grace, **imputes to me** the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ, **as if I had never sinned** nor been a sinner." (Q&A 60)

See also Belgic Confession, Articles 22–23, and Calvin, *Institutes* 3.11.2, where Calvin defines justification as "the acceptance with which God receives us into his favor as righteous men... the remission of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness."

---

## 2. The Biblical Case

**a) The meaning of "justify."** The Greek *dikaioō* and Hebrew *ṣādaq* (Hiphil) are typically declarative, used in courtroom settings:

- Luke 7:29: the people "justified God." They obviously did not infuse righteousness into God.

**b) God justifies the *ungodly*.** Romans 4:5 says God "justifies the ungodly." The person justified is, considered in himself, still ungodly at the moment of the verdict. That makes sense only if the ground of the verdict lies outside him.

**c) Imputation language.** Romans 4:3–8 uses *logizomai* ("count, reckon, credit") repeatedly, and David's blessing is on the man "to whom God counts righteousness apart from works."

**d) The great exchange.** 2 Corinthians 5:21 says Christ was "made sin," not by moral corruption but by imputation, so that "we might become the righteousness of God in him." The parallel suggests our righteousness is likewise reckoned.

**e) A righteousness not my own.** Philippians 3:9 speaks of "not having a righteousness of my own... but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God."

**f) Adam–Christ parallel.** Romans 5:18–19 says that through one man's obedience "the many will be made [*kathistēmi*, constituted/appointed] righteous." This is a representative, covenantal constitution, mirroring how Adam's sin was reckoned to his posterity.

# A Reformed Evaluation of Purgatory

From a Reformed perspective, this statement is **false** and was a central point of dispute in the Reformation. Here is why, along with a fair account of the view being rejected.

## 1. The Claim Being Evaluated

Catholic teaching (*Catechism of the Catholic Church* §§1030–1032; Council of Trent, Session 25) holds that those who die in God's grace but are "still imperfectly purified" undergo purification after death to attain the holiness needed for heaven. This purification is understood as:
- not a second chance for the unsaved,
- not the remission of the eternal guilt of sin (already forgiven), but
- the cleansing of remaining attachment to sin and the satisfaction of "temporal punishment."

Note that official Catholic teaching does not specify that "most" believers go to purgatory, though this is a common assumption.

## 2. The Reformed Confessional Position

The Reformed confessions explicitly reject purgatory:

- **Westminster Confession 32.1**: "The souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens... Besides these two places, for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none."
- **Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 37**: "The souls of believers are at their death made perfect in holiness, and do immediately pass into glory."
- **Heidelberg Catechism Q. 57**: "Not only shall my soul after this life be immediately taken up to Christ its head..."
- **Calvin, *Institutes* 3.5.6–10**: Calvin calls purgatory a "deadly fiction" that "makes void the cross of Christ."
- **Thirty-Nine Articles, Art. 22** (Anglican, with Reformed influence): "a fond thing, vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture."

## 3. Theological Objections

**a) The sufficiency of Christ's satisfaction.** Reformed theology holds that Christ bore the *entire* penalty for believers' sins, both eternal and temporal. "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb. 10:14). "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from *all* sin" (1 John 1:7). Any remaining penal satisfaction owed by the believer implies that Christ's work was incomplete.

**b) Justification by imputed righteousness.** The believer's standing before God rests on Christ's righteousness credited to them (Rom. 4:5–8; 2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 3:9), not on their own attained holiness. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 8:1). Fitness for heaven is grounded in Christ, not in a process of personal purification completed after death.

**c) Sanctification completed by God's act.** Reformed theology agrees that believers need to be made perfectly holy before entering God's presence (Heb. 12:14; Rev. 21:27). It holds that God accomplishes this *instantaneously* at death by sovereign grace, much as bodies will be transformed "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye" at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52). Glorification is God's gift, not a remedial process requiring suffering.

**d) Sola Scriptura.** Purgatory is judged to be a doctrine that developed through tradition, not one taught in canonical Scripture.

- **2 Corinthians 5:8**: To be "away from the body" is to be "at home with the Lord."

# A Reformed Evaluation of the Marian Dogmas

The statement combines three distinct claims: the **Immaculate Conception** (defined by Pius IX in 1854), Mary's **lifelong sinlessness**, and the **Bodily Assumption** (defined by Pius XII in 1950). Reformed theology rejects all three as doctrines, while affirming a high regard for Mary herself.

## What the Reformed Tradition Affirms About Mary

Reformed rejection of these dogmas is not disdain for Mary:

- **Theotokos.** The Reformed churches accept Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451). Mary is truly the mother of the one person who is God incarnate.
- **Virgin birth.** Christ was "conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary" (Apostles' Creed; WCF 8.2; Heidelberg Catechism Q35).
- **Blessedness.** "All generations will call me blessed" (Luke 1:48). Mary is honored as a model of faith and humble submission: "Let it be to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38).

The objection is to claims that go beyond Scripture and are bound on the conscience as necessary to salvation.

## 1. The Immaculate Conception

**The principle of authority.** The Reformed position rests on *sola Scriptura*. The Westminster Confession states that the whole counsel of God "is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture" (WCF 1.6). The Immaculate Conception is neither stated in Scripture nor deducible from it.

**The universality of original sin.** Scripture presents sin as universal among Adam's descendants: "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23); "death spread to all men because all sinned" (Rom 5:12). The Westminster Confession says original sin is "conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation" (WCF 6.3). Mary was conceived by ordinary generation, and Scripture makes no exception for her.

**Christ's unique sinlessness.** The New Testament singles out Christ as the one without sin (Heb 4:15; 7:26; 2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:22; 1 John 3:5). It never extends this to anyone else.

**The Christological argument does not require it.** A common argument holds that Christ needed a sinless mother to be sinless himself. Reformed theology answers that Christ's holiness is grounded in the Spirit's work at his conception: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you... therefore the child to be born will be called holy" (Luke 1:35). The Heidelberg Catechism (Q35–36) and Belgic Confession (Art. 18) locate Christ's sinlessness there. If a sinless mother were required, the same logic would demand a sinless grandmother, and so on without end.

**Historical development.** The doctrine was contested within the medieval Western church. Bernard of Clairvaux opposed a proposed feast of the Conception, and Thomas Aquinas held that Mary was sanctified in the womb after conception, not preserved from original sin at conception. Duns Scotus's argument for "preservative redemption" eventually prevailed, but the doctrine was formally defined only in 1854. To Reformed eyes, a dogma unknown or disputed by major Catholic doctors for centuries can hardly be apostolic tradition.

# A Reformed Evaluation of Transubstantiation

**Short answer:** The Reformed tradition rejects this statement. It affirms that believers truly partake of Christ's body and blood in the Supper, but denies that the bread and wine change substance.

## The Confessional Position

The Reformed confessions explicitly reject transubstantiation:

- **Westminster Confession of Faith (29.6):** Transubstantiation "is repugnant, not to Scripture alone, but even to common sense and reason; overthroweth the nature of the sacrament; and hath been, and is, the cause of manifold superstitions; yea, of gross idolatries."
- **Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 78):** "Just as the water of baptism is not changed into Christ's blood... so too the holy bread of the Lord's Supper does not become the actual body of Christ."
- **Belgic Confession (Art. 35)** and the **Second Helvetic Confession (ch. 21)** say the same.

## Main Reformed Arguments

**1. The nature of a sacrament.** A sacrament is a visible sign and seal of an invisible grace. If the sign is annihilated and replaced by the thing signified, the sacrament loses its structure. The bread must remain bread to function as a sign. Calvin argued that transubstantiation "destroys the sign."

**2. The interpretation of "This is my body."** Reformed theologians read Christ's words as *sacramental speech* (a form of metonymy), where the name of the thing signified is given to the sign. Scripture does this elsewhere: circumcision is called "the covenant" (Gen. 17:10), the lamb is called "the Passover" (Ex. 12:11), and Paul says "the rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:4). At the Last Supper Christ was physically present and holding the bread, which suggests the disciples did not understand him to be holding his own body in his hands.

**3. The ascension and Christ's true humanity.** This is central to the Reformed position. Christ's human body is a true, finite body, and it ascended and is now located in heaven at the Father's right hand (Acts 1:11; 3:21). A true human body cannot be present in substance on thousands of altars at once without compromising its genuine humanity. Reformed theologians see this as a Christological issue, tied to Chalcedon's insistence that each nature keeps its own properties.

**4. The finished sacrifice.** Hebrews stresses that Christ offered himself "once for all" (Heb. 7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–14). Transubstantiation is closely bound up with the Roman doctrine of the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, which the Reformed view as detracting from the sufficiency of the cross (HC Q. 80; WCF 29.2).

**5. Worship and idolatry.** If the elements are not Christ, then adoring the consecrated host means worshiping a creature. Hence the strong language in Heidelberg Q. 80 and WCF 29.4, which also rejects reserving and processing the elements.

**6. Philosophical dependence.** The doctrine, as defined at Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551), relies on an Aristotelian distinction between substance and accidents. Reformers argued that a dogma binding on consciences should not rest on a particular philosophical framework, and that the patristic witness is more varied than Rome claims.

## What the Reformed *Affirm*

The Reformed view is not mere memorialism (the view often associated with Zwingli). Following Calvin, most Reformed confessions teach a **real spiritual presence**:

- Believers "really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified" (WCF 29.7).
- The Holy Spirit unites believers to the ascended Christ, so that they are nourished by his true body and blood. Calvin called this a "mystery" he could "rather experience than understand."
- The emphasis is on the *sursum corda* ("lift up your hearts"). Christ is not brought down into the elements. Rather, the faithful are lifted up to him by the Spirit.
- The benefit is received **by faith**. Unbelievers receive only the outward elements, not Christ (WCF 29.8), in contrast with both Roman Catholic and Lutheran teaching.

## Summary Comparison

| View | Elements change? | How Christ is present |
|---|---|---|
| Roman Catholic | Yes, in substance | Bodily, under the appearances of bread and wine |
| Lutheran | No | Bodily, "in, with, and under" the bread |
| **Reformed** | **No** | **Truly but spiritually, by the Spirit, received through faith** |
| Memorialist | No | Mainly as remembrance |

# A Reformed Evaluation of "Limited Inerrancy"

The statement describes what is usually called **limited inerrancy** or **infallibility of purpose**. The historic confessional Reformed tradition rejects it, while granting that it raises real questions about interpretation. Below are the main lines of Reformed response, followed by the concerns that give the view its appeal and some notes on internal debate.

---

## 1. The Confessional Witness

The major Reformed confessions ground Scripture's authority in its divine origin, not in its subject matter:

- **Westminster Confession of Faith 1.4**: Scripture's authority "dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself) the author thereof."
- **WCF 1.5** speaks of "the entire perfection thereof" and its "infallible truth and divine authority."
- **Belgic Confession, Art. 5**: Reformed believers receive the canonical books "believing without any doubt all things contained in them."
- **Belgic Confession, Art. 7**: Scripture "fully contains the will of God."

The phrase "all things contained in them" is significant. The confessions do not divide Scripture into authoritative religious content and fallible historical or natural content. WCF 1.6 does say Scripture contains all things necessary for "faith and life," but that phrase describes Scripture's *sufficiency*, not a limit on its *truthfulness*.

## 2. The Theological Arguments

### a. The character of God
Reformed theology begins with the doctrine of God. If Scripture is truly God's Word, "breathed out" by God (2 Tim. 3:16), its truthfulness follows from the character of its Author, who "cannot lie" (Titus 1:2; Heb. 6:18). Affirming that God speaks erroneously in some domains raises a question: why trust him in others?

### b. Christ's view of Scripture
The Reformed argue that a Christian's doctrine of Scripture should follow Christ's own. Jesus treated historical details of the Old Testament as factual and authoritative:
- "Scripture cannot be broken" (John 10:35)
- Not "one jot or tittle" will pass away (Matt. 5:18)
- He treated Adam and Eve, Noah, Jonah, and Abraham as historical (Matt. 19:4–5; 24:37–39; 12:40; John 8:56–58)

B. B. Warfield argued that the church's doctrine of inspiration is simply the doctrine of Christ and the apostles.

### c. Redemption is historical
This is perhaps the strongest Reformed objection. Biblical faith is not timeless religious insight. It is the proclamation of what God has done in history. Covenant theology depends on real events: creation, the fall, the Exodus, the exile, the Incarnation, the crucifixion, the resurrection. Paul makes faith depend on a historical claim: "If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (1 Cor. 15:17). Likewise, his argument in Romans 5 about the two Adams presupposes a historical Adam. Separating "faith" from "history" therefore threatens the gospel itself, which is a report of history interpreted by God.

### d. Who draws the line?
If Scripture is authoritative only in "faith and practice," someone must decide which texts fall into that category. That authority then moves from Scripture to the interpreter, scholarly consensus, or the church. Reformed critics argue this undermines *sola Scriptura*: the reader becomes the judge of the Word rather than standing under it. The line also proves unstable. Sexual ethics, the historicity of miracles, and the resurrection have all been reclassified as "cultural" or "historical" by those who began with limited inerrancy.

### e. Organic, not mechanical, inspiration
Herman Bavinck and Abraham Kuyper stressed that God used the human authors' personalities, vocabularies, and cultural settings. Rather than implying error, this shows that God's sovereign providence shaped the authors and their situations so that their genuinely human words were also genuinely his. Divine and human authorship are not competitors.

# A Reformed Evaluation of Universalism

From a Reformed perspective, this statement would be judged **false**, both in its conclusion (all will be saved) and in its reasoning (that divine love rules out eternal punishment). Here is how a Reformed theologian would typically analyze it.

---

## 1. The Appeal to Scripture

Reformed theology holds to *sola Scriptura*, so the first question is not "What would a loving God do?" but "What has God revealed?" Several passages are read as teaching a final, eternal division:

- **Matthew 25:46**: "These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." The same word (*aiōnios*) describes both destinies. If the life is unending, so is the punishment.
- **John 3:36**: "Whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
- **2 Thessalonians 1:9**: Those who do not obey the gospel "will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord."
- **Revelation 20:10–15** and **Mark 9:43–48** use imagery of unending judgment.

Jesus himself is the most frequent teacher on hell in the New Testament, which makes it difficult to set "the loving Jesus" against the doctrine.

## 2. The Flaw in the Premise: Love Defined Apart from God

The statement assumes we already know what love must do, and then judges God by that standard. Reformed theology rejects this method on two grounds:

- **Divine simplicity and the unity of God's attributes.** God is not love *instead of* being holy and just. His love is a holy love and his justice a loving justice. Pitting one attribute against another misunderstands God's nature.
- **The Creator-creature distinction.** God's ways are not our ways (Isaiah 55:8–9). Human intuitions about fairness, shaped by sin, are not a reliable standard for judging God (Romans 9:20).

A Reformed thinker would also say that a God who never punished evil would not be more loving but less good. A judge who acquits the guilty is not merciful but corrupt (Proverbs 17:15).

## 3. The Gravity of Sin

Reformed theology stresses **total depravity**: all humanity is fallen in Adam, guilty, and unable to save itself (Romans 3:10–23; Ephesians 2:1–3). Following Anselm and Jonathan Edwards, many Reformed theologians argue that sin's seriousness is measured by the dignity of the one offended. Sin against an infinitely holy God merits an infinite penalty.

The universalist statement treats condemnation as something God would have to justify. The Reformed view reverses this. **Condemnation is what sinners deserve. Salvation is what requires explanation**, and the explanation is grace.

## 4. Grace Is Not Owed

If salvation were owed to everyone, it would no longer be grace. Reformed theology, especially the doctrine of **unconditional election** (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11–16), insists that God is free in bestowing mercy:

> "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion." (Romans 9:15)

The Canons of Dort (I.1) state that God would have done no injustice had he left the entire human race in sin and condemnation. That he saves anyone is astonishing mercy, not an obligation.

## 5. The Cross Refutes the Argument

The cross shows that God's love does not simply set aside justice. It satisfies justice:

> "It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." (Romans 3:26)

If a loving God could simply forgive everyone, the death of Christ would be unnecessary. Reformed **penal substitutionary atonement** holds that the cross is where divine love and justice meet. God loves sinners enough to bear their penalty himself, in the person of his Son. Love is displayed *through* justice, not *against* it.
